m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Install Python 3.12, Docker, and Git, or set up a GitHub Codespace that has all three.
  • Explain why this course pins one Python version across your laptop, your container, and CI.
  • Check each tool from a terminal and recognize what a working install prints.
  • Fix the setup errors people hit most: the Windows Store python alias, a stopped Docker engine, Docker socket permissions on Linux, and a missing venv package.

Here is a bug that has nothing to do with machine learning. A model is trained on a laptop with scikit-learn 1.8 and saved to a file. The server that loads it has scikit-learn 1.5. On load, scikit-learn raises an InconsistentVersionWarning, and if nobody reads the logs, the service keeps running with a model that may now compute different answers. No test caught it, because the tests ran on the laptop.

The code in this course will run in three places: your computer, a Docker container, and (from Module 5) a GitHub Actions runner. The fix for the bug above is to make all three agree, down to the exact Python and library versions. That's why this setup is fussier about versions than most.

#What you're installing and why

Tool What it does in this course Cost
Python 3.12 Trains models, runs the FastAPI service and the tests Free, open source
Docker Builds the service into an image and runs it as a container Docker Desktop is free for personal use, education, non-commercial open source, and small businesses; Docker Engine on Linux is open source
Git and a GitHub account Version history, and later CI/CD with GitHub Actions Free
A code editor Editing files; VS Code is a good free choice Free

Why Python 3.12 and not the newest release? The container in Module 2 starts from the official python:3.12-slim image, and the library versions this course pins (NumPy 2.1.3, pandas 2.2.3, and friends) publish ready-made packages for Python 3.12 and 3.13 but not 3.14. Matching your laptop to the container removes a whole category of "works on my machine" bugs.

Check your hardware before starting: a 64-bit computer, at least 8 GB of RAM if you're on Windows (Docker's stated minimum), hardware virtualization switched on, and several gigabytes of free disk for Docker images.

#Step 1: Install Python 3.12

Windows

  1. Open PowerShell and run winget install --id Python.Python.3.12 -e. If winget isn't available, download the Windows installer (64-bit) for Python 3.12.10 from python.org and tick Add python.exe to PATH on the first screen.
  2. Close PowerShell and open a new window so it picks up the new PATH.
  3. Run py -3.12 --version. The py launcher lets you choose a version even when several are installed.

macOS

  1. Either download the macOS 64-bit universal2 installer for Python 3.12.10 from python.org and run it, or, if you use Homebrew, run brew install python@3.12.
  2. Open a new Terminal window.
  3. Run python3.12 --version.

Linux

  1. Ubuntu 24.04 ships Python 3.12. Install it with the venv module (Ubuntu packages it separately): sudo apt update && sudo apt install python3.12 python3.12-venv.
  2. Run python3.12 --version.
  3. On other distributions, install Python 3.12 from your package manager, or use pyenv to build it.

Chromebook

Skip to No admin rights or on a Chromebook below. A GitHub Codespace gives you Python 3.12, Docker, and Git in the browser.

Any 3.12.x is fine. If you see 3.13.x, the course still works on your machine, but your container will run 3.12, so prefer 3.12 locally if you can.

#Step 2: Install Docker

Windows

  1. Docker Desktop runs Linux containers inside WSL 2. In an administrator PowerShell, run wsl --install, then restart. (If WSL is already installed, wsl --update brings it up to date.)
  2. Download Docker Desktop for Windows from docs.docker.com and double-click Docker Desktop Installer.exe.
  3. On the Configuration page, choose Use WSL 2 instead of Hyper-V if it asks. Finish the wizard and select Close.
  4. Docker Desktop doesn't start by itself. Search for Docker Desktop in the Start menu, open it, and accept the Docker Subscription Service Agreement.
  5. Requirements: 64-bit Windows 10 (22H2) or Windows 11 (23H2 or later). Home and Education editions run Linux containers, which is all this course needs.

macOS

  1. Check your chip under Apple menu › About This Mac, then download Docker Desktop for Mac with Apple silicon or with Intel chip.
  2. Double-click Docker.dmg and drag the Docker icon into Applications.
  3. Open Docker.app from Applications and accept the agreement. The whale icon in the menu bar shows that the engine is running.
  4. Docker Desktop supports the current macOS release and the two before it.

Linux

  1. Install Docker Engine (no Desktop needed). The most reliable route is Docker's own apt repository; follow "Install Docker Engine on Ubuntu" at docs.docker.com. For a personal dev machine, Docker's convenience script also works: curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com -o get-docker.sh then sudo sh get-docker.sh.
  2. To run docker without sudo, add yourself to the docker group: sudo groupadd docker, sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, then log out and back in (or run newgrp docker). This group grants root-level access to the machine, so only do it on a computer you control.

Chromebook

The Codespace setup below includes Docker. Personal Chromebooks with the Linux development environment can also install Docker Engine with the Linux steps, but school-managed Chromebooks usually block it.

Now prove the engine works. hello-world is a tiny official image whose only job is to print a message:

The first two lines appear only the first time, while Docker downloads the image. Run it again and they disappear, because the image is now cached on your machine.

#Step 3: Git and a GitHub account

Windows

Run winget install --id Git.Git -e, or download Git for Windows from git-scm.com. Accept the installer's defaults. Open a new terminal afterwards.

macOS

Run git --version in Terminal. If Git isn't installed, macOS offers to install the Command Line Developer Tools; accept, and Git comes with them.

Linux

Run sudo apt install git (or your distribution's equivalent).

Chromebook

Git is already installed in every Codespace.

Then create a free account at github.com and tell Git who you are. GitHub can hide your real email: under Settings › Emails, turn on Keep my email addresses private and copy the @users.noreply.github.com address it shows you.

Any recent version number is fine.

#No admin rights or on a Chromebook: use a GitHub Codespace

A Codespace is a Linux machine in GitHub's cloud with VS Code in your browser. GitHub Free accounts get a monthly allowance (listed as 120 hours of compute time and 15 GB-month of storage at the time of writing), and if you have no payment method on file, GitHub stops usage at the limit instead of charging you. Codespaces stop after 30 minutes of inactivity by default, which protects the allowance.

  1. On GitHub, click New repository, name it late-delivery, tick Add a README file, and create it. (Modules 2 to 4 build this one project: a service that predicts whether a food delivery will arrive late.)
  2. In the repository, choose Add file › Create new file, type the name .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, paste the configuration below, and commit it.
  3. Click the green Code button, open the Codespaces tab, and create a codespace on main.

The image line pins Python 3.12. Without this file, Codespaces uses its default "universal" image, which currently defaults to a newer Python. The docker-in-docker feature installs a Docker engine inside the codespace, so docker run hello-world works in its terminal. forwardPorts makes your API reachable from the browser in Module 2.

#When something goes wrong

⚠️ Watch out

Windows: Python was not found; run without arguments to install from the Microsoft Store. Windows ships placeholder python.exe aliases that open the Store. Use py -3.12 instead, or turn the aliases off under Settings › Apps › Advanced app settings › App execution aliases (switch off the two python entries).

⚠️ Watch out

Cannot connect to the Docker daemon ... Is the docker daemon running? (on Windows the message mentions a pipe such as dockerDesktopLinuxEngine instead). The docker command works, but the engine behind it is stopped. Open Docker Desktop and wait for it to say the engine is running; on Linux, run sudo systemctl start docker. On Windows, if Docker Desktop itself complains about WSL or virtualization, run wsl --update and check that virtualization is enabled in your BIOS/UEFI settings.

⚠️ Watch out

Linux: permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket. Your user isn't in the docker group yet, or you added it but haven't logged out and back in. Run groups to check, and repeat the group steps in Step 2 if docker isn't listed.

⚠️ Watch out

Ubuntu: The virtual environment was not created successfully because ensurepip is not available. Ubuntu splits venv into its own package. Run sudo apt install python3.12-venv, delete the half-made .venv folder, and create it again.

#Check yourself

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Your laptop has Python 3.14 and your Dockerfile starts FROM python:3.12-slim. What's the real risk?

  • New Python versions do remove and change things, and compiled libraries publish separate packages per version, so "it installed on my laptop" says little about the container.

  • Exactly. You'd be testing a different environment from the one you ship. Matching versions makes your local tests evidence about production.

  • Docker doesn't look at your laptop's Python at all; the image brings its own.

Show answer

B. Exactly. You'd be testing a different environment from the one you ship. Matching versions makes your local tests evidence about production.

2docker --version prints a version, but docker run hello-world says it cannot connect to the Docker daemon. What's wrong?

  • If it weren't, docker --version would fail with "command not found".

  • The docker command is only a client that talks to the engine. Start Docker Desktop (or the docker service on Linux) and try again.

  • A missing image gives a "pull access denied" or "not found" error, not a daemon connection error.

Show answer

B. The docker command is only a client that talks to the engine. Start Docker Desktop (or the docker service on Linux) and try again.

3On a school Chromebook without Linux enabled, which setup covers every lesson for $0?

  • Docker Desktop isn't available for ChromeOS.

  • It runs in the browser, includes Python, Docker, and Git, and stops at the free allowance instead of billing you.

  • A notebook can train a model, but it can't build or run Docker images, which you'll need from Module 2.

Show answer

B. It runs in the browser, includes Python, Docker, and Git, and stops at the free allowance instead of billing you.

Key takeaways

  • The course pins Python 3.12 everywhere because the container uses python:3.12-slim.
  • docker run hello-world printing "Hello from Docker!" proves both the client and the engine work.
  • The docker command is a client; most "cannot connect" errors mean the engine is stopped.
  • No admin rights? A Codespace with the devcontainer.json above is a complete, free setup.

#Further reading

  • Docker Desktop for Windows: install guide (opens in a new tab): the current system requirements and the WSL 2 backend options.
  • Install Docker Engine on Ubuntu (opens in a new tab): the apt-repository method, and how to remove conflicting older packages first.
  • Introduction to dev containers (opens in a new tab): what devcontainer.json controls in a Codespace.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create a project folder with its own virtual environment on any operating system.
  • Install exact library versions from requirements.txt and requirements-dev.txt.
  • Run a smoke test that trains, saves, reloads, and serves a tiny model.
  • Start a real API server with uvicorn and call it from a browser.
  • Run Python 3.12 inside a Docker container.

By the end of this page you should have three passing checks. A model trains, goes to disk, comes back, and gives identical predictions. A web API answers GET /health with {"status": "ok"}. And a container started from python:3.12-slim reports Python 3.12. Each check exercises one layer of the service you'll build in Module 2, so if one fails, you know exactly which layer to fix.

#Step 1: Make the folder and a virtual environment

A virtual environment (venv) is a private folder of packages for one project. Without one, every project on your computer shares a single set of libraries, and upgrading scikit-learn for one project silently changes another.

Windows

In PowerShell:

If PowerShell says the script cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system, run Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned once, answer Y, and activate again.

macOS

Linux

Chromebook

In your Codespace, the repository folder is already open. In the terminal at the bottom:

Your prompt now starts with (.venv). While it's active, python and pip mean the venv's copies on every operating system, so the rest of the course just says python. Run deactivate to leave, and activate again each time you open a new terminal.

#Step 2: Pin the libraries

Create two files in the project folder. The first lists what the running service needs; the second adds tools only developers need (the test client and pytest). Keeping them apart means the Docker image in Module 2 won't carry test tools into production.

== means "exactly this version". These are the versions that produced every output you'll see in this course, so your numbers should match the pages. The -r line includes the first file, so one command installs both:

Notice that pip installs more packages than you listed, such as starlette and anyio. Those are dependencies of your dependencies. They aren't pinned yet; Module 4 shows how to lock the complete set.

#Step 3: Check the environment

Save this as check_setup.py and run it with python check_setup.py. It checks the things the smoke test can't see: the Python version, and whether docker and git are on your PATH.

sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix is how Python itself tells whether it's running inside a venv: the prefix points at .venv, while the base prefix points at the Python you created it from. A FIX on that line means you forgot to activate.

#Step 4: The smoke test

This program touches every library the service will use. Save it as smoke_test.py and run it.

Two things to notice. joblib.dump wrote the fitted model, coefficients and all, into smoke.joblib, and joblib.load rebuilt an identical object from it. And TestClient sent a real HTTP request to the app without starting a server or opening a port: it calls the app directly in the same process. That's why it's the workhorse for testing APIs in this course.

#Step 5: Start a real server

The test client is great for tests, but you also want to see the API the way a user's program will. Save this as hello.py:

Then start it with uvicorn, the web server that runs FastAPI apps. hello:app means "the object called app in hello.py", and --reload restarts the server whenever you save a change.

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/health (opens in a new tab) in your browser and you'll see {"status":"ok"}. Each request adds a log line such as "GET /health HTTP/1.1" 200 OK in the terminal. Now open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs (opens in a new tab): FastAPI generates an interactive page listing every endpoint, with a Try it out button. You'll use it to send test predictions in Module 2. Press Ctrl+C to stop the server.

In a Codespace, a pop-up offers to open the forwarded port 8000; the Ports tab lists it too. Forwarded ports are private to your GitHub account by default.

#Step 6: Run Python 3.12 in a container

Last check. This starts a throwaway container from the official slim Python image, runs one line of Python inside it, and deletes the container when it exits (--rm):

The last line must start with 3.12; the patch number depends on when you pulled the image. Notice that the container's Python has nothing to do with the Python on your laptop. The image carries its own operating system files and interpreter, which is exactly why containers make deployments repeatable.

⚠️ Watch out

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fastapi' when you run the smoke test usually means the venv isn't active, so python is your system Python. Look for (.venv) in your prompt. If it's missing, activate again; if it's there, run python -m pip install -r requirements-dev.txt once more.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1Why does requirements-dev.txt exist instead of putting pytest in requirements.txt?

  • It can; -r just includes another file. The split is about what goes where.

  • Smaller images build faster, and every package you don't ship is one you don't have to patch.

  • pip resolves all requirements together; file names don't affect order.

Show answer

B. Smaller images build faster, and every package you don't ship is one you don't have to patch.

2The smoke test printed GET /health -> 200, but no server was running. How?

  • Nothing listened on any port; you could run the test with port 8000 already in use.

  • It builds a real HTTP request and response, but skips the network, which makes tests fast and repeatable.

Show answer

B. It builds a real HTTP request and response, but skips the network, which makes tests fast and repeatable.

Key takeaways

  • One project, one venv, activated in every new terminal.
  • Pin exact versions with ==, and keep test-only tools in requirements-dev.txt.
  • TestClient tests an API in-process; uvicorn serves it for real on port 8000.
  • docker run --rm python:3.12-slim ... gives you a clean Python 3.12, whatever your laptop has.

#Further reading

  • venv: creation of virtual environments (opens in a new tab): the official reference, including how activation works on each shell.
  • FastAPI: first steps (opens in a new tab): the smallest app, /docs, and how path operations work.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Create the folder layout the whole course uses, with a script you can re-run safely.
  • Write a .gitignore that keeps environments, caches, and secrets out of Git.
  • Commit in small, described steps and check git status before every commit.
  • Clean up stopped containers and unused images.
  • Debug by location: a Python traceback, an HTTP status code, or a container that won't start.

A first push to GitHub that takes twenty minutes is a classic. The culprit is almost always .venv: thousands of files of other people's libraries, compiled for one operating system, useless to anyone who clones the repository. GitHub also blocks any single file over 100 MB, so a large model file can make the push fail outright. Both problems are prevented by one small file, written before the first commit.

#The layout every module adds to

Each module fills in part of this tree. You don't need all of it today, but creating it now means later lessons can say "put this in app/" without explanation.

The rule behind it: code that serves predictions lives in app/, code that produces the model lives at the top level, and outputs (data/, models/, registry/) live in their own folders so they're easy to ignore, copy into an image, or hash.

This script creates the folders and starter files. It never overwrites a file that already exists, so it's safe to run again. Save it as scaffold.py in the project folder and run python scaffold.py.

exist_ok=True makes mkdir quietly succeed if the folder is already there, and the if path.exists() check protects files you've edited. Scripts that are safe to run twice are called idempotent, and you'll want that property in every setup and deployment script in this course: a pipeline that fails halfway should be safe to simply run again.

#What goes in Git

The .gitignore above encodes three decisions:

  • Environments and caches stay out. .venv can be rebuilt from requirements.txt in a minute, and it only works on the machine that made it.
  • Secrets stay out, always. API keys go in a .env file or the hosting platform's secret settings. A key pushed to a public repository should be treated as leaked even if you delete it a minute later, because the old commit still contains it.
  • Generated data stays out. make_data.py uses a fixed random seed, so it rebuilds the same data/orders.csv every time.

The model file is a judgment call. This course's model is a few kilobytes, so committing models/ is fine for now and lets a hosting service build your image straight from the repository. Once artifacts reach megabytes, they belong in a registry with a recorded hash, which is exactly what Module 4 builds.

#A commit rhythm that keeps history useful

Commit whenever one thing works: the scaffold, then the training script, then the API. Each commit is a point you can return to. Run git status before every commit; it's the cheapest bug check there is.

Read that list before running git add .. If .venv/ appears in it, your .gitignore isn't working (check that it's in the project root and spelled with the leading dot). Empty folders such as data/ don't appear at all, because Git tracks files, not folders. Write commit messages that finish the sentence "This commit will…": "Add /health endpoint", not "stuff" or "fix".

#Keep Docker from eating your disk

Every image you build stays on disk until you remove it, and Module 2 builds a lot of them. These commands show what's there and clean it up.

Both prune commands ask for confirmation first. Neither touches running containers or tagged images you're still using.

#Debug by asking "where did it fail?"

Most errors in this course come from one of three places, and each has its own first move.

A Python traceback is read from the bottom. The last line names the exception and the message; the lines above it show the chain of calls that led there, most recent last. Here's one you'll see if you start the API before training a model:

The last line says everything: the file models/model.joblib doesn't exist relative to where you ran the command. Either the model hasn't been trained yet, or you ran the program from the wrong folder. Run python train.py from the project root, then try again.

These are the messages you're most likely to meet, with their usual causes:

What you see What it usually means Fix
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fastapi' The venv isn't active Activate it; check for (.venv) in the prompt
[Errno 48] Address already in use (macOS), [Errno 98] (Linux), [WinError 10048] (Windows) Another server already holds port 8000 Stop it with Ctrl+C in its terminal, or start with --port 8001
Status 422 from the API The request body failed validation Read detail in the response: it names the field and the rule
curl: (7) Failed to connect to localhost port 8000 Nothing is listening there Start the server, or publish the container's port with -p 8000:8000
Bind for 0.0.0.0:8000 failed: port is already allocated An older container still holds the port docker ps, then docker stop it

⚠️ Watch out

A server running in the background is the most common invisible cause of "it's still showing the old version". If your change doesn't appear, check docker ps and your other terminal windows for a server you started earlier.

#Asking for help so people can answer

When you're stuck for more than 20 minutes, ask, and include enough for someone to reproduce the problem without your computer:

Writing this down solves a surprising share of problems before you send it.

Check your understanding

2 questions

1git status lists .venv/ under "Untracked files". What should you do before git add .?

  • GitHub stores whatever you push. It has no idea which folders are environments.

  • Untracked files that match an ignore pattern aren't listed, so .venv/ showing up means the pattern isn't being applied.

  • You need the venv to work; it just shouldn't be committed.

Show answer

B. Untracked files that match an ignore pattern aren't listed, so .venv/ showing up means the pattern isn't being applied.

2Your API returns status 500 for every prediction. Where is the most useful information?

  • The server deliberately returns only "Internal Server Error", so attackers learn nothing about your code. That also means it tells you nothing.

  • The full traceback is written to the server's log. The last line names the real exception.

  • The URL shows what you asked for, not why the server failed.

Show answer

B. The full traceback is written to the server's log. The last line names the real exception.

Key takeaways

  • Serving code goes in app/, model-making code at the top level, and outputs in their own folders.
  • Ignore .venv, caches, secrets, and data you can regenerate; commit small model files for now.
  • Run git status before every commit, and commit each time one thing works.
  • Read tracebacks from the bottom, read detail on a 422, and read the server's log on a 500.

#Further reading

  • gitignore documentation (opens in a new tab): the full pattern rules, including negation with ! and folder-only patterns.
  • Docker: prune unused objects (opens in a new tab): what each prune command removes, and how to filter by age.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Save a complete scikit-learn pipeline with joblib, and explain why saving only the classifier breaks.
  • Write a Pydantic request model whose constraints document and enforce the API's input contract.
  • Build a FastAPI app with /health and /predict that loads the model once, at startup.
  • Choose between 200, 422, 503, and 500 for each outcome a prediction service can have.
  • Explain what a container image adds that a requirements.txt file can't.

In a notebook, this line works:

It works for exactly one person, the one who remembers that the columns are distance in kilometres, number of items, hour of day, and whether it's raining, in that order. A teammate's app calling your model needs answers to questions the notebook never had to ask. Is distance in kilometres or miles? Is hour 0 to 23 or 1 to 24? What comes back, and what does 1 mean? What happens when someone sends hour = 25? And who loads the model, and when?

A prediction service answers every one of those questions in code. This lesson builds one for the course project: a model that predicts whether a food delivery will arrive late.

#Save the whole pipeline, not just the classifier

Here is the model. The data is generated (with a fixed seed) so you can rebuild it exactly; each row is an order, and late records whether it arrived after its promised time.

The pipeline does two jobs. The ColumnTransformer turns raw columns into the numbers the classifier expects: it scales distance and items using the mean and standard deviation it measured on the training data, and it turns hour into 13 on/off columns, one for each hour it saw. Then logistic regression predicts. Those learned means and categories are part of the model just as much as the coefficients are.

So the artifact you save is the whole pipeline:

Now watch what happens if you save only the last step, which is a common first attempt:

The classifier was trained on 16 engineered columns (2 scaled, 13 hour flags, 1 rain flag) and has no idea how to make them from 4 raw ones. Worse versions of this bug don't crash: save the classifier and re-fit a fresh scaler on the server's incoming data, and the shapes match but every prediction is subtly wrong. Saving the pipeline makes training and serving run the same preprocessing code.

⚠️ Watch out

Only load model files you made. joblib uses Python's pickle format, and loading a pickle can run arbitrary code. Treat a .joblib file from the internet like an unknown .exe. Also load it with the same scikit-learn version that saved it: a mismatch triggers InconsistentVersionWarning, and the results aren't guaranteed. That's why Module 1 pinned scikit-learn==1.8.0 and why the next lesson records the version next to the model.

#Write the contract down with Pydantic

The service's input contract is the set of requests it promises to handle. Pydantic lets you write that contract as a class, and FastAPI enforces it on every request before your code runs.

Read the second line of output closely. Pydantic's default "lax" mode converted the string "6.5" to a float and "yes" to True, because those conversions are unambiguous. The third request had three separate problems, and Pydantic reported all of them at once, each with its location and the rule it broke. A client developer can fix everything in one round trip.

extra="forbid" deserves a word. By default Pydantic silently drops fields it doesn't know. If a client sends "tip": 2 believing tips affect lateness, silently ignoring it hides a misunderstanding; rejecting it surfaces one.

#Load once, predict many

Now the service itself. Two design decisions are visible in the code: the model loads in a lifespan function that runs once when the server starts, and the endpoints are plain def functions.

Loading at startup means a missing or corrupt model file stops the server from starting at all, which is the failure you want: loud, immediate, and before any customer is affected. Loading inside predict() would repeat the disk read on every request and turn a broken file into a stream of errors hours later.

Why def and not async def? predict_proba is ordinary CPU work that blocks while it runs. FastAPI runs plain def endpoints in a thread pool, so one slow prediction doesn't freeze the server's event loop for everyone else. Use async def only when the function awaits something, such as a network call.

Send it real requests with the test client. The with block matters: it's what makes the test client run the lifespan.

A long, rainy, rush-hour order comes back with a high probability of being late, plus the model version that produced the answer. That version field costs nothing to include and is the first thing you'll want when someone reports a strange prediction.

#Errors are part of the contract

A good service fails in ways a client program can act on. Predict the status code before you run this: the order below has hour set to 25.

FastAPI returned 422 without ever calling predict(), and the body says which field broke which rule. These are the four outcomes worth designing for:

Status Meaning Who produces it
200 Here's the prediction Your endpoint
422 Your request breaks the contract; fix it and retry FastAPI, from the Pydantic model
503 I'm up but can't predict right now; retry later Your endpoint (HTTPException)
500 Bug on the server; details are in the server log only Any unhandled exception

The difference between 422 and 503 tells the client whose problem it is. Never return 200 with an "error" field inside: monitoring, load balancers, and retry logic all read the status code, not your JSON.

⚠️ Watch out

Forgetting with around TestClient skips the lifespan. The model never loads, so a test that looks correct gets 503:

This is also why /health checks the model instead of always answering "ok". A health check that reports healthy while the model is missing will keep sending traffic to a server that can't do its job.

#Why the service goes in a container

Your service now depends on Python 3.12, eight pinned libraries, your code, and a model file, and they must all be present together. requirements.txt covers the libraries but not the Python version, operating system packages, or the model file. A container image bundles all of it into one artifact with a name and tag, such as late-delivery:1.0.0. A container is a running instance of that image, and the same image runs the same way on your laptop, a CI runner, or a cloud host.

The recipe for the image is a Dockerfile. Here's the core of the one you'll build in the next lesson:

Each instruction adds a layer: start from Python 3.12 on Debian, install the pinned libraries, then copy in the code and the model. The --host 0.0.0.0 matters inside a container, and the next lesson shows exactly what goes wrong without it.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You deploy model.named_steps["clf"] instead of the whole pipeline. What does the first request do?

  • It never gets that far with raw columns: the classifier can't even accept them.

  • The scaling and one-hot encoding lived in the pipeline's first step. Without it, nothing turns raw order fields into the columns the classifier was trained on.

  • The preprocessing exists only in the ColumnTransformer you left behind.

B. The scaling and one-hot encoding lived in the pipeline's first step. Without it, nothing turns raw order fields into the columns the classifier was trained on.

2A client sends {"distance_km": 6.5, "items": 3, "hour": "18", "raining": true} with hour as a string. What happens?

  • Strict mode would reject it, but Pydantic's default lax mode accepts a string that is clearly an integer.

  • The conversion is unambiguous, so lax mode allows it. "eighteen" or "18.5" would get a 422.

  • predict() only ever sees the validated Order, where hour is already an int.

Show answer

B. The conversion is unambiguous, so lax mode allows it. "eighteen" or "18.5" would get a 422.

3Why load the model in the lifespan function instead of at the top of predict()?

  • Endpoints can read files; it's just a poor place to do it.

  • Both latency and failure behaviour improve: problems surface before the server takes traffic.

  • joblib.load is an ordinary function; the lifespan is async because FastAPI requires that shape.

Show answer

B. Both latency and failure behaviour improve: problems surface before the server takes traffic.

4The model file loads fine, but a bug in your endpoint raises KeyError. What status does the client see?

  • 503 is a status you choose deliberately with HTTPException. Unhandled exceptions don't produce it.

  • Unhandled exceptions become "Internal Server Error". The client learns nothing about your code, which is the safe default.

  • A Pydantic model is the input contract: types, ranges, and extra="forbid", enforced before your code runs.

  • 422 means "the client sent something wrong", 503 means "the server can't predict right now", and 500 means a bug.
  • A container image packages Python, libraries, code, and model so they always travel together.

What you'll learn

  • Split the work into scripts with one job each: make data, train, serve, test.
  • Save model metadata (version, metrics, library version, threshold) next to the model file.
  • Write API tests that check the contract, the error cases, and one behaviour the model must have.

Here's where this lesson ends: a container running on your machine that answers this request.

Everything that produces that answer is built from files you can read, rerun, and version:

Each cell below is one file in your project. Save it under the name in its title and run it from the project root (the late-delivery folder). On this page the cells run in order, and later cells read the files earlier ones wrote.

#Step 1: Generate the data

In a real system this script would be a query against your orders database. Keeping it separate from training means you can swap the data source without touching the model code.

#Step 2: Train and write the model's metadata

The training script writes two files. model.joblib is the fitted pipeline. model.json is everything a person or program needs to know about it without unpickling it: which version it is, which features it expects, the decision threshold, how well it scored, and which scikit-learn version made it.

The metrics come from the 25% of rows the model never trained on. Writing them down now matters later: in Module 4 you'll compare a retrained model against these numbers before deciding whether to replace this one.

#Step 3: Write the service

This is the complete app/main.py. It's the service from the last lesson with three upgrades: the model folder comes from an environment variable (so a container can point it elsewhere), the version and threshold come from model.json instead of being typed into the code, and each Field has a description that appears on the /docs page.

columns=meta["features"] pins the column order to the one recorded at training time. The ColumnTransformer selects columns by name, so order wouldn't break it today, but the moment someone swaps in a model that takes a plain NumPy array, an unpinned order silently scrambles every feature.

A quick in-process check before writing tests, using the same order as the opening example:

You can also try it with a real server before going near Docker: uvicorn app.main:app --reload, then open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs (opens in a new tab), expand POST /predict, click Try it out, and send an order.

#Step 4: Test the contract and one behaviour

Tests for a model service check three kinds of thing: the contract (shapes, types, status codes), the error cases, and at least one behaviour any sane model must show. That last one catches problems a status-code test can't, such as a model trained on shuffled labels.

In your project, run them with python -m pytest from the project root. The python -m form puts the current folder on Python's import path, which is what lets from app.main import app find your package; a bare pytest command may fail with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'app'.

#Step 5: Write the Dockerfile and .dockerignore

Line by line, the decisions:

  • FROM python:3.12-slim matches your venv's Python exactly. "Slim" is Debian with the extras removed; pin it to 3.12-slim, never latest, so a rebuild next year doesn't quietly switch Python versions.
  • PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 sends log lines straight to docker logs instead of holding them in a buffer, so you see errors when they happen. PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 skips writing .pyc files the container doesn't need.
  • requirements.txt is copied and installed before the code. Docker caches each layer and reuses it if its inputs haven't changed. Because the slow pip install layer depends only on requirements.txt, editing app/main.py rebuilds in seconds instead of reinstalling scikit-learn.
  • Only requirements.txt is installed, not the dev file, so pytest and httpx stay out of production.
  • USER appuser runs the server as an ordinary user. If someone finds a hole in your code, they land in an account that can't modify the system.
  • HEALTHCHECK has Docker call /health every 30 seconds. The slim image has no curl, so the check uses Python's built-in urllib, which exits with an error on any non-2xx response.
  • --host 0.0.0.0 makes uvicorn listen on every network interface in the container. Its default, 127.0.0.1, accepts connections only from inside the container itself.

The .dockerignore file keeps the build context small and stops local junk from leaking into the image:

Without it, COPY instructions and the build context would drag in your entire .venv (hundreds of megabytes compiled for your OS) and possibly a .env file full of secrets.

Run it. -p 8000:8000 publishes the container's port 8000 on your machine's port 8000, and --name gives the container a name you can type:

⚠️ Watch out

The container is up but curl gets an empty reply or "connection reset". Check the log line Uvicorn running on http://.... If it says 127.0.0.1, the server only accepts connections from inside the container; add --host 0.0.0.0 to the CMD. If it says 0.0.0.0, check that you passed -p 8000:8000 to docker run.

  • Docker rebuilds a layer and everything after it only when that layer's inputs change. Code changes far more often than dependencies, so it goes last.

What you'll learn

  • Spot requests a loose schema accepts that a real service must reject.
  • Write Pydantic constraints, a 503-aware health check, and a validated batch endpoint.
  • Add middleware that logs one JSON line per request with a request ID and duration.
  • Find the problems in a Dockerfile by reasoning about layers, users, and networking.
  • Measure, rather than guess, the cost of loading a model inside the request handler.

#Warm-up: what does a loose schema let through?

Run this setup cell first. It rebuilds the course model and starts with a deliberately loose service: the request model has types but no ranges.

Before running the next cell, write down the status code you expect for each request.

Types alone caught two problems. The other two are worse than errors: a delivery to a negative distance and an order placed at hour 40 both got confident-looking probabilities. The OneHotEncoder ignored the unknown hour 40, and the scaler happily scaled −3 km. A model always returns a number, so it's the contract's job to refuse inputs that make no sense.

#Exercise 1: Tighten the contract

Write an Order model that rejects all three bad cases from the warm-up (negative distance, hour 40, and an unknown field such as "tip"), and a strict_app that uses it. Allow distances above 0 and up to 50 km, 1 to 50 items, and hours 0 to 23.

Need a hint?

Field(gt=0, le=50) means "greater than 0, at most 50". Unknown fields are allowed by default; one line in model_config changes that. Each 422 body has a detail list whose items carry a loc.

Show solution

The constraints live in the schema, so FastAPI rejects bad requests before strict_predict runs, and the /docs page shows the allowed ranges to every client developer.

#Exercise 2: Make the health check tell the truth

Add a GET /health to a new app, health_app, that returns {"status": "ok", "model_version": ...} when the model is loaded and 503 when it isn't. Prove both branches: call it once inside with TestClient(...) and once without with.

Need a hint?

raise HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="...") produces the error response. The lifespan only runs when the test client is used as a context manager.

Show solution

Load balancers and Docker's HEALTHCHECK stop sending traffic to an instance whose health check fails. A check that only proves "the process is running" would keep routing requests to a server that can't predict.

#Exercise 3: Score many orders in one request

A partner wants to send up to 100 orders at once. Add POST /predict/batch to strict_app taking {"orders": [...]} (1 to 100 Order objects) and returning one probability per order, in order, computed with a single predict_proba call. Requests with 0 or 101 orders must get 422.

Need a hint?

A Pydantic model can have a field of type list[Order], and Field(min_length=1, max_length=100) limits the list's length. score() already accepts a list of dicts.

Show solution

One predict_proba call on 100 rows costs barely more than one call on 1 row, because the fixed overhead (building a DataFrame, running each pipeline step) is paid once. The size limit protects the server: without it, one request with a million orders could hold a worker for minutes. Module 3 measures this trade-off properly.

#Exercise 4: Log one JSON line per request

When something goes wrong in production, you search logs. Build logged_app, a copy of strict_app's /predict with HTTP middleware that, for every request, writes one JSON line with a request ID, method, path, status code, and duration in milliseconds, and returns the ID in an X-Request-ID response header. If the client sent its own X-Request-ID, reuse it so one ID can follow a request across services.

Need a hint?

@logged_app.middleware("http") decorates an async def that receives request and call_next; response = await call_next(request) runs the endpoint. Add middleware to a fresh app: Starlette raises RuntimeError: Cannot add middleware after an application has started if the app has already served a request, which strict_app has. Use logging with a StreamHandler(sys.stdout) rather than print, so the log level and destination can change without code edits.

Show solution

Notice that the 422 was logged too: middleware wraps everything, including validation failures that never reach your endpoint. Logging the body itself is tempting but risky, since real request bodies often contain personal data; log identifiers and measurements instead.

#Exercise 5: Review a broken Dockerfile

A teammate's Dockerfile builds, but it has at least five problems. Find them, say what each one causes, and write a fixed version. (There's no code to run; reason about it.)

Need a hint?

Go line by line and ask: will this be the same next year? What happens to the cache when I edit one Python file? What ends up inside the image? Who does the server run as? Where does uvicorn listen by default?

Show solution
  1. python:latest changes whenever a new Python ships, so a rebuild can silently switch versions (and the full image is several times larger than slim). Pin python:3.12-slim.
  2. COPY . /app before installing means any code edit invalidates the cache and reinstalls every library. It also copies .venv, .git, and any .env secrets unless a .dockerignore excludes them.
  3. requirements-dev.txt ships pytest and httpx to production. Install requirements.txt only.
  4. RUN python train.py trains a new, untested model at every build and needs the training data inside the image. Train outside, test, then copy the artifact in.
  5. CMD uvicorn app.main:app listens on uvicorn's default 127.0.0.1, which is unreachable from outside the container. It's also the shell form, which runs under /bin/sh -c; the JSON exec form runs uvicorn directly, so docker stop signals reach it and it can shut down cleanly.
  6. No USER, so the server runs as root.

#Exercise 6: Measure the cost of loading per request

Someone suggests loading the model inside the handler "so it's always fresh". Measure what that costs. Build two apps that differ only in where joblib.load happens, time 20 requests to each, and do it for the small logistic regression and for a 150-tree random forest.

Your numbers will differ, and both columns include the test client's own overhead per request; the gap between the columns is what matters.

Need a hint?

Write a function build_apps(path) that returns both apps: one loads the model into a variable before defining its endpoint, the other calls joblib.load(path) inside its endpoint. Send one warm-up request before starting the timer.

Show solution

For a 4 KB model the reload costs a few milliseconds, which is how this mistake survives code review: it doesn't show up until the model grows. With the forest, most of each request is spent reading the file again. Big neural networks take seconds to load, so per-request loading would make the service unusable. "Always fresh" is the job of a deployment (a new container with the new model), not of every request.

#Challenge: Refuse to start with the wrong scikit-learn

A model saved with one scikit-learn version and loaded with another may predict differently. Write guarded_lifespan, which reads model.json first and raises a RuntimeError naming both versions if sklearn_version doesn't match the installed one. Prove it by writing a model.json that claims 1.5.2, show that the app refuses to start, then restore the real file.

Need a hint?

Do the check before yield. An exception raised there makes with TestClient(app) raise too, the same way uvicorn would print Application startup failed. Exiting. and stop. Keep the original file's text in a variable so you can put it back.

Show solution

Failing at startup turns a silent accuracy problem into a deploy that visibly doesn't come up, and the error message says exactly how to fix it: rebuild the image with the version the model was trained on, or retrain.

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Define batch, online, streaming, and edge inference, and give a workload that fits each.
  • Measure latency as percentiles (p50, p95, p99) and explain why the mean hides problems.
  • Show why scoring rows in bulk is far cheaper per row than one request at a time.
  • Use Little's law to estimate how many requests a service has in flight, and how many instances it needs.
  • Compare always-on, scale-to-zero, and scheduled costs, and name free hosts that fit each mode honestly.

Two delivery companies, two mistakes. The first scores tomorrow's two million scheduled orders by sending each one to its prediction API, one HTTP request at a time, every night. The job takes most of the night and the API runs at full tilt for it. The second company computes its late-delivery warnings in a nightly batch, so when a customer adds a third pizza to the cart at 6 p.m. in the rain, the warning they see was computed from a different, drier order the night before.

Both companies have a fine model. They picked the wrong serving mode: the way predictions get from the model to whoever needs them.

#Four ways to deliver a prediction

  • Batch. Score many rows on a schedule, store the results, and look them up later. Tomorrow's scheduled orders can be scored at 2 a.m., because everything the model needs is known in advance.
  • Online (also called real-time, or request/response). A client sends one request and waits for the answer. The checkout page asks "will this order be late?" the moment the cart changes.
  • Streaming. A consumer reads events from a stream (Apache Kafka is the common open-source choice) as they happen and writes predictions to another stream, usually within seconds. Each GPS ping from a driver updates that order's arrival estimate, and nobody is waiting on a request.
  • Edge. The model runs on the user's device: a phone, a browser, a car. There's no network round trip, it works offline, and the data never leaves the device. A driver's app that flags risky routes in a tunnel needs this.
Mode When it computes Input freshness What the user waits for What you operate
Batch On a schedule As of the last run A lookup (fast) A scheduled job and a results table
Online On each request Live The model, every time An always-reachable API
Streaming On each event Seconds old Nothing; results are pushed A consumer and a message broker
Edge On the device Live, local The device's own CPU Model files shipped inside an app

Many real systems mix them. A common pattern serves batch scores when they're fresh and falls back to the online API when they aren't; you'll build that in the practice lesson.

#Latency and throughput are different numbers

Latency is how long one prediction takes. Throughput is how many predictions you finish per second. They pull in different directions, and you can see it with the course model. This cell trains it and builds 200,000 orders to score:

Now score 300 of them one at a time, the way an online API does, and then all 200,000 in a single call:

Two things to see. First, the bulk call is thousands of times cheaper per row. Almost all of a single prediction is fixed overhead: building a DataFrame, checking columns, running each pipeline step. Bulk scoring pays it once. A real API adds HTTP parsing, JSON, and a network round trip on top, which makes the gap bigger still. That's the first company's mistake in numbers.

Second, look at the spread of the single-row latencies. The p50 (median) is what a typical request sees. The p99 is the latency that 1 in 100 requests exceeds, and it sits well above the median even in this tiny loop, because of garbage collection, other programs on the machine, and cache misses. Service-level objectives are written in percentiles ("p95 under 100 ms") because a page that makes several calls hits the slow tail far more often than 1% of the time.

⚠️ Watch out

Averages hide the tail. A mean of 8 ms can sit on top of a p99 of 40 ms, and a handful of very slow requests barely moves the mean. Always report p50, p95, and p99 together, measured over enough requests (hundreds at least) that the p99 means something.

#How many requests are in flight? Little's law

When requests arrive faster than one worker can finish them, they queue. Step through this tiny simulation: a request arrives every 20 ms, and each prediction takes 30 ms.

Every request waits 10 ms longer than the one before, forever. The worker is asked for 30 ms of work every 20 ms, which is 150% utilization, so the queue never drains. Real services fall over this way: latency climbs, clients time out and retry, and the retries add more load.

Little's law makes this precise. In a steady system, the average number of requests in flight equals the arrival rate times the average time each one spends inside:

L = λ × W (requests in flight = arrivals per second × seconds per request)

At 200 requests per second with 40 ms per request, there are on average 200 × 0.040 = 8 requests in progress at once. If one instance handles 4 at a time and you want headroom (say, run at 60% of capacity so bursts don't cause queues), you need ⌈8 / (4 × 0.6)⌉ = 4 instances:

Notice the third row: doubling latency nearly doubles the instances you need, even with the same traffic. Making each prediction faster is often cheaper than buying more servers.

#What each mode costs

Cloud providers bill in three main shapes, and each mode matches one:

  • Always-on instances bill for every hour they exist, busy or idle. Online APIs with steady traffic usually live here.
  • Scale-to-zero platforms (often called serverless) bill only while handling requests, but the first request after an idle period pays a cold start while a container boots and loads the model.
  • Scheduled jobs bill only while they run. Batch scoring lives here.

The prices below are made-up round numbers to show the shape of the comparison; real prices vary by provider and change often, so check the pricing page before deciding anything.

The batch job is about a hundred times cheaper, if the predictions can be computed in advance. That condition is the whole decision.

#Free places to run each mode

These are the free options that fit this course's Docker service and scripts. Free tiers change, so treat the details as "true when this was written" and check each provider's page.

  • Online API: Render's free web services. Render builds a web service from your Dockerfile (choose Docker as the language) and offers a Free instance type: 0.1 CPU and 512 MB of RAM, 750 free instance hours per workspace each month, and an ephemeral filesystem. A free service spins down after 15 minutes without traffic, and the next request waits about a minute while it starts again. Fine for a demo; not for a checkout page.
  • Batch jobs: scheduled GitHub Actions workflows. A workflow with on: schedule runs on a cron expression in UTC, at most every 5 minutes, and only on the default branch. Standard GitHub-hosted runners are free for public repositories; private repositories get a monthly allowance. Scheduled runs can start late when GitHub is busy (the top of every hour is the busiest time), and in public repositories they're disabled after 60 days without repository activity.
  • Hugging Face Spaces. Spaces host ML demos, and the free CPU Basic hardware provides 2 vCPUs and 16 GB of RAM. At the time of writing, though, creating a Docker or Gradio Space on that hardware requires a paid PRO account; free accounts can create static Spaces and up to two Gradio Spaces on ZeroGPU. For this course's Docker service, that makes Render the free choice.
  • Edge. There's no host to pay for: the model ships inside the app. scikit-learn models are usually converted to a portable format such as ONNX first, so the device doesn't need Python.
  • Streaming needs a message broker running all the time. You can run Kafka locally in Docker to learn it, but there's no free always-on option worth recommending, so this course treats streaming as a design choice you should recognize rather than one you deploy.

⚠️ Watch out

A free tier's cold start is part of your latency. If your p99 target is 200 ms and the service sleeps after 15 minutes idle, the first user after a quiet period waits about a minute. Measure the cold start along with the warm latency, and say which one your numbers describe.

#Choosing, as a flowchart

The first question does most of the work. If the inputs are known ahead of time, batch is almost always simpler and cheaper, and the only thing to check is that results won't be too stale by the time they're used.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A bank re-scores every customer's churn risk once a week for its marketing team. Which mode fits?

  • The inputs are known in advance and nobody is waiting on an answer, so a weekly job is the cheapest and simplest option.

  • An always-on API would sit idle all week and then be hammered with millions of calls. That's the first company's mistake.

  • Marketing reads results in a central system; there's no device that needs the model.

Show answer

A. The inputs are known in advance and nobody is waiting on an answer, so a weekly job is the cheapest and simplest option.

2Your API's mean latency is 12 ms, and the p99 is 450 ms. What does that tell you?

  • 1 in 100 requests takes nearly half a second, and pages that make several calls hit that tail much more often than 1% of the time.

  • A big gap between p50 and p99 usually points at something intermittent: garbage collection, a cold cache, a noisy neighbour, or queueing under bursts.

  • A few slow requests barely move the mean, which is exactly why the mean hides them.

Show answer

B. A big gap between p50 and p99 usually points at something intermittent: garbage collection, a cold cache, a noisy neighbour, or queueing under bursts.

3Traffic stays at 100 requests per second, but a new model raises latency from 50 ms to 150 ms. By Little's law, what happens to requests in flight?

  • Requests in flight depends on traffic and time in the system.

  • L = λW: 100 × 0.05 = 5 before, 100 × 0.15 = 15 after. Without more capacity, queues build.

  • Nothing here batches requests; each still waits for its own turn.

Show answer

B. L = λW: 100 × 0.05 = 5 before, 100 × 0.15 = 15 after. Without more capacity, queues build.

4A demo runs on a free host that sleeps after 15 idle minutes. A reviewer opens it after lunch, and the first request takes 60 seconds. What happened?

  • The next requests are fast, so the model fits; only the first one was slow.

  • Scale-to-zero saves money while idle and charges you in latency on the first request back.

Show answer

B. Scale-to-zero saves money while idle and charges you in latency on the first request back.

Key takeaways

  • Batch scores ahead of time, online answers each request, streaming reacts to events, and edge runs on the device.
  • Bulk scoring is far cheaper per row than single requests, because most of a single prediction is overhead.
  • Report latency as p50, p95, and p99; the mean hides the slow tail.
  • Little's law, L = λW, turns traffic and latency into the concurrency you must provision.
  • Free hosting today: Render for a sleeping online API, GitHub Actions for scheduled batch jobs; Hugging Face Docker Spaces now need a paid plan.

What you'll learn

  • Write a batch scorer that reads in chunks, validates columns, and replaces its output file atomically.
  • Stamp every stored prediction with the model version and the time it was computed.
  • Benchmark an API's latency percentiles and draw them as a histogram.
  • Compare batch and online throughput on the same model and the same machine.
  • Schedule the batch job with a GitHub Actions cron workflow, and deploy the API to Render's free tier.

The late-delivery model has two customers. The operations team wants a risk score for every one of tomorrow's 50,000 scheduled orders by 7 a.m., so they can add drivers on the worst routes. The checkout page wants a score for one cart, right now. Same model file, two serving modes. By the end of this lesson you'll have both, measured:

The exact numbers depend on your machine. The shape doesn't: batch wins on throughput by a wide margin, and only online can answer a cart that didn't exist last night.

#Step 1: Start from Module 2's artifacts

If you finished Module 2, models/model.joblib and models/model.json already exist in your project. This cell recreates them on this page so the rest of the lesson has something to load.

#Step 2: Make tomorrow's scheduled orders

In production this file would come from a database query run just before scoring. Here a script generates 50,000 orders with an ID, the day they're scheduled for, and the four features. raining is tomorrow's forecast, which is the catch with batch scoring: forecasts change, and a score computed at 2 a.m. can't know that.

#Step 3: Write the batch scorer

The scorer has four habits worth copying into any batch job:

  1. It reads the input in chunks, so memory stays flat whether the file has fifty thousand rows or fifty million.
  2. It checks the columns before scoring and fails with a message that names what's missing.
  3. It writes every row with the model version and the time it was scored, so anyone reading a prediction can tell where it came from and how old it is.
  4. It writes to a temporary file and renames it at the end. A crash halfway leaves yesterday's complete file in place instead of half of today's.

Look at what landed on disk, and at what the operations team actually needs from it:

Running the script twice produces the same file name with the same rows (only scored_at changes), so a job that's retried after a failure doesn't create duplicates. That property, being safe to rerun, matters more for scheduled jobs than speed does.

#Step 4: Benchmark the online API

Now the other path. Here is the Module 2 service, trimmed to /predict:

The benchmark sends 300 different orders, one after another, and times each full request: JSON encoding, validation, the DataFrame, the model, and the response. A few warm-up requests come first so one-time setup costs don't pollute the numbers.

This measures the service's own processing time on your machine. A real client also pays for the network, which adds anywhere from under a millisecond (same data center) to hundreds (another continent). When you report latency, say which one you measured.

#Step 5: Put the two modes side by side

The online path could go faster with more workers and parallel clients, but each request still pays the full fixed overhead. The batch path pays it once per 10,000-row chunk. Use batch for what can be scored ahead of time, and keep the API for what can't.

#Step 6: Schedule the batch job with GitHub Actions

Save this as .github/workflows/nightly-batch.yml. It runs every night at 07:30 UTC (cron times are always UTC unless you set a time zone), and workflow_dispatch adds a Run workflow button on the repository's Actions tab so you can test it without waiting until tonight.

The steps mirror what you ran by hand: get the code, install the same Python and the same pinned libraries, make the input, score it, and keep the output as a downloadable artifact on the run's summary page. In a real system the last step would write to a database or a storage bucket instead, using a secret stored in the repository's Settings › Secrets and variables › Actions.

⚠️ Watch out

Scheduled workflows run late sometimes, and stop silently in quiet public repositories. GitHub may delay schedule runs when Actions is busy, especially at the top of the hour, which is why this one runs at :30. Scheduled workflows also run only on the default branch, and in a public repository they're disabled after 60 days without activity. If the 7 a.m. deadline is real, have the job record when it finished and alert when it hasn't.

#Step 7: Deploy the online API to Render's free tier

Render sets a PORT environment variable (10000 by default) and expects your server to listen on it, on 0.0.0.0. Change the last line of the Module 2 Dockerfile so the port comes from the environment, with 8000 as the fallback for local runs:

The exec form ["sh", "-c", ...] is needed because only a shell expands ${PORT:-8000}. The word exec then replaces the shell with uvicorn, so the stop signal from the platform reaches uvicorn directly and it shuts down cleanly. Build and run locally once to check nothing broke (docker build -t late-delivery:1.0.0 . and docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 late-delivery:1.0.0), then push to GitHub with models/ committed.

Then, in the Render Dashboard:

  1. Click New › Web Service and connect your GitHub account, then choose the late-delivery repository.
  2. Set Language to Docker. Render finds the Dockerfile in the repository root.
  3. Where the form asks for a plan (Render calls it the instance type or compute plan), choose Free.
  4. Under Advanced, set the health check path to /health.
  5. Click Create Web Service and watch the build log. When it finishes, the service has a public URL ending in onrender.com.

Measure the cold start and the warm latency separately with curl's timing output (-w prints the status code and total time):

Those two lines are an example of the pattern you'll see after the service has been idle for 15 minutes: the first request waits for the container to start, and the next one is fast. The warm number includes the round trip over the internet, so it's far above the in-process latency from Step 4.

#The finished project

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does score_batch.py write to *.tmp and rename the file at the end?

  • Speed isn't the point; the rename happens once, at the end.

  • A rename on the same disk swaps the old file for the new one in a single step. Until it happens, readers see the complete previous file.

  • pandas appends to any open file handle; the extension doesn't matter.

Show answer

B. A rename on the same disk swaps the old file for the new one in a single step. Until it happens, readers see the complete previous file.

2An analyst finds an odd risk score in the predictions file a week from now. Which columns let them trace it?

  • It says which order, but not which model scored it or when.

  • Together they say exactly which artifact produced the number and how stale its inputs (like the rain forecast) might have been.

  • That's the decision, not where it came from.

Show answer

B. Together they say exactly which artifact produced the number and how stale its inputs (like the rain forecast) might have been.

3The Render service's first request after lunch took 49 seconds, and the next took 0.19 seconds. Which number belongs in your write-up?

  • They happen after every 15 idle minutes on the free tier, so a low-traffic service hits them constantly.

  • It's real, but reporting only it hides how the service behaves once it's running.

  • Cold and warm latency describe different user experiences, and the free tier's spin-down makes the cold one common.

Show answer

C. Cold and warm latency describe different user experiences, and the free tier's spin-down makes the cold one common.

Key takeaways

  • A batch job should chunk its input, check columns, stamp each row with model version and time, and replace its output atomically.
  • Benchmark the API end to end with warm-up requests, and report p50, p95, and p99.
  • Batch beats online on throughput by orders of magnitude because it pays the fixed overhead once per chunk.
  • A GitHub Actions schedule with workflow_dispatch runs the batch job for free; expect occasional delays.
  • On Render, listen on 0.0.0.0:$PORT, use a /health check, and measure cold and warm latency separately.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a --date option so the scorer can re-score a past day, then make the output file name include the date.
  • Have the workflow open a GitHub issue automatically when scoring fails.
  • Run the API benchmark against your Render URL with 50 requests and compare its percentiles with the in-process ones.

#Further reading

  • pandas: iterating through files chunk by chunk (opens in a new tab): chunksize, iterator, and reading only the columns you need.
  • Render: Docker on Render (opens in a new tab): building from a Dockerfile, the Dockerfile path setting, and build secrets.
  • GitHub Actions workflow syntax (opens in a new tab): every key used in the workflow above.

What you'll learn

  • Match workloads to batch, online, streaming, or edge from their requirements.
  • Judge a latency objective with percentiles, not the mean.
  • Size an online service for normal traffic and for bursts with Little's law.
  • Measure how batch size trades latency for throughput, and choose a size under a budget.
  • Make a batch job safe to rerun after a crash, and combine batch and online scoring in one lookup.

#Warm-up: name the mode

For each workload, pick batch, online, streaming, or edge, and say which requirement decided it.

  1. A streaming service recommends tomorrow's homepage rows for each of 40 million users.
  2. A card payment must be approved or declined within 300 ms while the customer waits.
  3. A factory camera checks every part on a conveyor belt; the factory's internet link drops several times a day.
  4. Each driver's GPS ping (one every 5 seconds) should update that order's arrival estimate on the customer's screen.
  5. A school district predicts next semester's enrolment per school, once a term.
  6. A note-taking app suggests tags while you type, and must work on a plane.
Show solution
  1. Batch. Every input (each user's history up to tonight) is known in advance, and nobody waits on the answer. Scoring 40 million users online would cost far more for the same result.
  2. Online. The input (this transaction) didn't exist until now, and someone is waiting with a hard deadline.
  3. Edge. It must keep working without the network, and sending video for every part off-site would be slow and expensive.
  4. Streaming. Predictions are triggered by a continuous flow of events, not by anyone asking.
  5. Batch. Once a term, inputs known ahead of time: the simplest possible case.
  6. Edge. "Works on a plane" means the model must run on the device.

#Setup

Run this once. It trains the course model and defines the order generator the exercises use.

#Exercise 1: Does the service meet its objective?

The team's objective is p95 ≤ 50 ms and p99 ≤ 150 ms. Here are 1,000 measured request latencies. Compute the mean, p50, p95, and p99, and decide whether the objective is met. Then explain why the mean alone would have misled you.

Need a hint?

np.percentile(values, [50, 95, 99]) returns all three at once. Check each half of the objective separately.

Show solution

Two percent of requests take 150 to 400 ms. That's enough to blow the p99 completely, but it adds only about 5 ms to the mean, which still looks healthy at 26 ms. The slow 2% are usually a specific cause worth hunting: a cold cache, a garbage-collection pause, or one slow dependency.

#Exercise 2: How many instances?

Peak traffic is 120 requests per second, the mean time per request is 50 ms, and each instance can work on 4 requests at once. The team keeps instances at or below 60% busy. How many instances are needed at peak? Marketing plans a promotion that could triple traffic for an hour: how many then?

Need a hint?

Little's law uses the mean time in the system: L = λ × W. Then divide by the usable concurrency per instance (4 × 0.6) and round up, because you can't run 2.5 instances.

Show solution

Two cautions. Little's law describes averages, so bursts within a second need the headroom you built in with the 60% target. And if latency rises under load (it usually does, as queues form), W grows too, so size from latency measured at the target load, not at idle.

#Exercise 3: Pick a micro-batch size

Some online services collect requests for a few milliseconds and score them together (micro-batching). Measure how long predict_proba takes for batches of 1, 4, 16, 64, 256, and 1,024 rows. Print the total time and the cost per row for each. Then set a latency budget of twice the single-row time (a request may wait at most about one extra request's worth of time for its batch) and choose the largest batch that fits.

Your timings will differ; the pattern of nearly flat total time with falling cost per row is what to look for.

Need a hint?

Time each size several times (say 20) and take the median, so one slow run doesn't decide the answer. Use make_orders(1024, seed=1)[FEATURES] and slice it with .iloc[:size].

Show solution

The total time grows far more slowly than the batch size, so the cost per row falls by hundreds of times between 1 row and 1,024. That's the fixed overhead again. (On a busy machine the timings jump around; the falling cost per row shows through anyway.) Micro-batching spends a little latency, the wait to fill the batch, to buy a lot of throughput. If your budget were tighter than a single row's time, no batch size would help, and you'd need a faster model or faster hardware.

#Exercise 4: Make the batch job resumable

A nightly job scoring 60,000 orders in 6 chunks crashes on chunk 3. Rerunning from scratch wastes the work already done, and appending to a half-written file creates duplicates. Write score_in_parts(frame, out_dir, chunk_rows, fail_at=None) that writes each chunk to its own file (part-00000.csv, part-00001.csv, ...), skips parts that already exist, and raises when it reaches the chunk number fail_at. Run it once with fail_at=3, then again without it, and finally combine the parts.

Need a hint?

Write each part to a temporary name and rename it only when complete, so a crash mid-part never leaves a file that looks finished. The existence check then means "this part is done".

Show solution

The second run does only the remaining half. This works because chunk boundaries are deterministic (same input, same chunk_rows, same parts) and each part is all-or-nothing. If the input could change between runs, you'd also record a hash of it and start over when it differs, which is Module 4's topic.

#Exercise 5: Where do always-on and pay-per-request break even?

Use these made-up prices: an always-on instance costs $0.05 per hour (730 hours a month); a scale-to-zero platform charges $2.00 per million requests and nothing while idle. At how many requests per month do they cost the same? What's that as an average rate per second? Print the monthly cost of each option at 1, 10, and 50 million requests.

Need a hint?

The always-on cost doesn't depend on traffic. Set the two monthly costs equal and solve for the number of requests. A 30-day month has 30 × 24 × 3600 seconds.

Show solution

Below about 7 requests per second on average, scale-to-zero is cheaper with these prices; above it, always-on wins. Cost isn't the whole answer, though: scale-to-zero buys its savings with cold starts, so a low-traffic service with a strict p99 might pay for always-on (or a minimum of one warm instance) anyway.

#Exercise 6: Serve batch scores when fresh, online when not

Combine the two modes. Write get_risk(order, batch_table, now) that returns the stored batch score if one exists for the order, is less than 12 hours old, and was computed with the same raining value the order has now. Otherwise it scores the order online. Return the probability and which path answered.

Need a hint?

Store raining and scored_at in each batch row, so you can compare them at lookup time. A dict keyed by order_id is a fine stand-in for a database table.

Show solution

What matters is which path answers each case. This hybrid gets batch's low cost for the common case and online's freshness for the rest. The key design choice is the staleness rule: here, age plus the one input known to change (weather). Pick rules from inputs that actually move, and record which path answered each request so you can see how often the fallback fires.

#Challenge: Turn the decision flowchart into tested code

Write choose_mode(workload) for a dictionary with three keys: inputs_known_in_advance, must_work_offline, and trigger ("request" or "event"). It should return "batch", "edge", "online", or "streaming" following the flowchart from the Notes lesson. Then write unit tests for at least four workloads from the warm-up and run them so the results print.

Need a hint?

Check the conditions in the same order as the flowchart; the order matters when more than one is true. unittest.TextTestRunner(stream=sys.stdout, verbosity=2) prints each test's name and result.

Show solution

The last test pins down a decision the flowchart makes implicitly: when inputs are known in advance, batch wins even if offline operation is also possible. Writing that as a test means nobody can reorder the if statements later without noticing.
