m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • List the five things that together identify a trained model, and why "latest" identifies none of them.
  • Fingerprint a data file and a model file with SHA-256, and predict which changes alter the hash.
  • Apply a semantic-versioning convention to models, and separate immutable versions from movable aliases.
  • Write a registry record that links a model version to its data, code, parameters, environment, and metrics.
  • Map those ideas onto MLflow's tracking server and model registry.

The incident report has one line under "model":

Which one is that? "latest" was retrained four times last month. Nobody can say which training data it saw, which commit of train.py built it, what its test score was, or which version it replaced, so nobody can say whether rolling back would help. The team spends the first two hours of the incident reconstructing history instead of fixing anything.

The cure is boring and completely effective. Every model gets a version that never changes meaning, and every version gets a written record of where it came from.

#What it takes to name a model exactly

A trained model is the output of a function with five inputs. Change any one, and you can get a different model:

The registry record is where all six identifiers get written down together, along with the metrics. Code already has a version system (Git). Environments are pinned by requirements.txt and the Docker base image. Data and artifacts are the gaps this lesson fills, and the tool for both is the same: a content hash.

#Fingerprint the data with a content hash

SHA-256 reads a file's bytes and produces a 64-character hex string. The same bytes always give the same string. Any change, however small, gives a completely different string, and nobody knows how to find two different files with the same one. That makes the hash a fingerprint: store 64 characters, and you can later prove whether a file is exactly the one you trained on.

Flipping one label out of 2,000 changed every character of the hash, which is exactly what you want from a fingerprint. Shuffling the rows changed it too, even though the set of rows is identical, because the file's bytes are in a different order. hashlib.file_digest (Python 3.11 and newer) reads the file in pieces, so it works on files far bigger than memory.

⚠️ Watch out

The hash covers bytes, not meaning. Opening the CSV in a spreadsheet and saving it again can change number formatting or line endings, and the hash changes even though no value did. That's a feature for reproducibility: it tells you the file isn't the one you trained on. If you need "same rows regardless of format or order", compute a canonical fingerprint from the parsed data instead; the practice lesson builds one.

#Same inputs, same bytes

Now hash the model. Train it twice from the same file, and once from the shuffled file:

Runs A and B produced byte-identical files. That's a strong, cheap reproducibility test: if retraining from the recorded inputs doesn't reproduce the recorded artifact hash, some input wasn't pinned (an unseeded split, a different library version, data that changed underneath you).

Run C is a different file. The solver added up the same numbers in a different order, and floating-point arithmetic isn't perfectly associative, so the coefficients differ in their last digits. The predictions agree to many decimal places, so for most purposes A and C are the same model. But "the same model" is a judgment; "the same bytes" is a fact, and facts are what an incident review needs.

#Version numbers people can reason about

A hash identifies an artifact, but nobody wants to say "roll back to d3a9be76". People need names that also carry meaning. Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) was invented for software libraries, where it describes API compatibility. For models, you have to define what the parts mean, and the most useful convention ties them to the service contract:

Bump When Example
MAJOR (2.0.0) The request or response contract changes; clients must change Adding a required restaurant_id feature, or switching distance to miles
MINOR (1.1.0) Same contract, different predictions Retrained on new data, new hyperparameters, a different algorithm, a new threshold
PATCH (1.0.1) Predictions identical for every input Fixing a typo in the metadata, repackaging the same weights

Two rules make versions trustworthy. A version is immutable: once 1.1.0 is registered, its artifact never changes, and a fix becomes 1.1.1 or 1.2.0. And a deployment refers to a version through an alias, a movable label such as champion (serving now) or challenger (being evaluated). Promoting a model moves the alias; rolling back moves it back. The versions underneath never change, so the history stays true.

"latest" fails both rules. It isn't a version (it moves), and it isn't a deliberate alias (it moves whenever anyone trains anything). Docker image tags have the same problem: late-delivery:latest can point at a different image tomorrow. Every image also has an immutable digest (sha256:..., shown by docker images --digests), and docker pull late-delivery@sha256:... always gets exactly that image.

#A registry is a table of records

A model registry stores, for every version, the artifact plus a record of where it came from, and keeps track of which version each alias points at. The record is the part that answers the incident review's questions. Here is the one for the model you just trained:

Every question from the incident report now has an answer in one file: which data (the hash), which code (the commit), what configuration, which environment, how good it was, and what it replaced (parent). On this page the code isn't in a Git repository, so the commit reads unknown, and the runner uses Python 3.13; in your project you'll see a real commit and 3.12.x. The -dirty suffix matters: it marks a model trained from code with uncommitted changes, which no commit can reproduce.

The registry itself can be as simple as a folder of these files, which is what you'll build next lesson. Larger teams use a registry service.

#The same ideas in MLflow

MLflow is a widely used open-source platform with two parts that matter here. Tracking records each training run's parameters, metrics, input datasets, and artifacts. The model registry turns a logged model into a named, versioned entry with aliases and tags. It isn't installed on this page, so the code below is shown rather than run; it follows the current MLflow 3 API. Install it in your dev environment only (python -m pip install mlflow); the serving image doesn't need it.

To browse runs and registered models, start the tracking server and open http://localhost:5000 (opens in a new tab):

Each idea from this lesson has an MLflow counterpart. Runs record params, metrics, tags, and datasets; log_input stores a dataset with a digest that MLflow computes for you. registered_model_name creates the next version of a named model. MLflow numbers versions with plain integers, so the semantic version goes in a tag. Aliases work as described above, and models:/late-delivery@champion always loads whichever version the alias points to. MLflow once used fixed "stages" (Staging, Production) for this; stages have been deprecated since MLflow 2.9 in favour of aliases and tags.

#Model cards: the record written for people

A registry record is for machines and incident reviews. A model card, an idea from a 2019 paper by Mitchell and colleagues, is the short document for people deciding whether to use the model: what it's for, what it isn't for, what data it learned from, how it performs (including on important subgroups), and its known limitations. A card for this model would include lines like these:

The best cards are generated from the registry record plus a few hand-written sentences, so the numbers can't drift from the truth. You'll generate one next lesson.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1You open data/orders.csv in a spreadsheet and click Save without changing any values. You hash it again. What happens?

  • The hash sees bytes, not values. Saving can change number formatting, quoting, or line endings.

  • That's the hash doing its job: the file is no longer byte-for-byte the one recorded. If you must edit data by hand, re-record its hash and treat it as new data.

  • They can; that's exactly why this mistake is common.

Show answer

B. That's the hash doing its job: the file is no longer byte-for-byte the one recorded. If you must edit data by hand, re-record its hash and treat it as new data.

2You change the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.4 without retraining. Under this lesson's convention, which version bump is it?

  • PATCH is for changes that leave every output identical. The late field now flips for some orders.

  • Clients still send and receive the same fields, but some answers differ, so it's a new behaviour under the same contract.

  • MAJOR is reserved for contract changes that force clients to change their code.

Show answer

B. Clients still send and receive the same fields, but some answers differ, so it's a new behaviour under the same contract.

3The serving config says alias: champion. You promote 1.2.0, and an hour later you need to roll back. What changes?

  • Versions are immutable, so rollback is just pointing the alias at a version that already exists and was already tested.

  • That would make "1.2.0" mean two different things, which destroys the history the registry exists to keep.

  • Unnecessary and risky: the previous artifact is still in the registry, byte for byte.

Show answer

A. Versions are immutable, so rollback is just pointing the alias at a version that already exists and was already tested.

4Retraining from a record's exact data file, commit, and environment gives a different artifact hash. What does that tell you?

  • For this pipeline, two runs from identical inputs gave byte-identical files.

  • Typical culprits: an unseeded random split, a library version that differs, or code with uncommitted changes (a -dirty commit).

  • SHA-256 treats every file as bytes; it's exactly as reliable for .joblib as for .csv.

Show answer

B. Typical culprits: an unseeded random split, a library version that differs, or code with uncommitted changes (a -dirty commit).

Key takeaways

  • A model is pinned by five inputs (data, code, config, environment) plus its artifact; record all of them.
  • SHA-256 fingerprints exact bytes: any edit, reorder, or re-save changes it.
  • Retraining from identical recorded inputs should reproduce the artifact hash; if it doesn't, something wasn't pinned.
  • Versions are immutable and carry meaning (MAJOR = contract, MINOR = behaviour, PATCH = nothing observable); aliases like champion move.
  • MLflow provides the same pieces: runs, registered model versions, tags, and aliases loaded with models:/name@alias.

#Further reading

  • MLflow Model Registry (opens in a new tab): versions, aliases, tags, and why stages were deprecated.
  • Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 (opens in a new tab): the original specification for software, worth reading to see what this lesson adapted.
  • Model Cards for Model Reporting (opens in a new tab): the paper that introduced model cards, with two example cards.

What you'll learn

  • Register model versions as immutable folders, each with the artifact and a JSON record.
  • Record content hashes for every training file and for the artifact.
  • Keep aliases in a file whose history is only ever appended to.
  • Promote a retrained candidate only after comparing it with the champion on a fixed holdout.
  • Load models by alias, verifying the artifact hash before unpickling, and generate a model card from the record.

When this lesson is done, your project will have a registry you can read with any text editor, and a service that loads whatever the champion alias points to:

There's no server and no database: a folder in your repository and about 80 lines of Python. That's enough to see every moving part of a registry clearly, and each function maps onto an MLflow call (there's a table at the end).

#Step 1: Data for two months, and a fixed holdout

The team trained version 1.0.0 on January's orders. February's orders have now arrived. Every version will be scored on the same frozen holdout file, so their metrics are comparable.

#Step 2: Register immutable versions

register() is the heart of the registry. Three details carry the weight:

  • It refuses to overwrite an existing version. Immutability isn't a promise in a README; it's an exception.
  • It builds the version in a temporary folder and renames it into place at the end, so a crash never leaves a half-registered version that looks complete.
  • It hashes every training file and the artifact it just wrote, and records the parent version it replaces.

Register January's model as 1.0.0, and then try to register 1.0.0 a second time:

#Step 3: Aliases with a history that's never rewritten

Aliases live in one small JSON file. current says where each alias points now; history records every move with the reason and time. The history is only appended to, never edited, so "what was serving at 14:05 on Tuesday?" always has an answer.

set_alias checks that the version exists, so a typo like "1.1" fails immediately instead of pointing production at nothing.

#Step 4: Retrain, compare on the holdout, and promote through a gate

Now retrain on January plus February. The request and response contract hasn't changed (same features, same output), so by the convention from the Notes lesson this is a MINOR bump: 1.1.0, with 1.0.0 as its parent.

Registering a version doesn't deploy it. Promotion is a separate, deliberate step with written rules. This gate allows a tiny drop (0.002 AUC is within the noise of a 1,000-row holdout) but refuses a real regression or any change to the feature list:

#Step 5: Serve by alias, and refuse a tampered artifact

The service now asks the registry for "whatever champion points to" instead of a hard-coded file. Before unpickling, it checks the artifact's hash against the record. That catches a corrupted download or an edited file, and because unpickling can run code, it means an artifact that isn't the one you registered is never even opened.

Plug it into the FastAPI lifespan. /health now reports both the version and the start of the artifact hash, so anyone can check what's serving without logging into the server.

Now simulate the file being altered after registration: one extra byte at the end of 1.1.0's artifact.

One byte was enough. In a container, that RuntimeError makes uvicorn print Application startup failed. Exiting., the container stops, and the health check never goes green, so the bad artifact never takes traffic.

#Step 6: Roll back by moving the alias

Suppose 1.1.0 misbehaves in production. Rollback doesn't rebuild or retrain anything; it points champion back at the version it replaced, which is recorded in the history:

Three moves, all visible. The 1.1.0 folder is untouched, so it can be investigated, fixed as 1.1.1 or 1.2.0, and promoted again later.

#Step 7: Generate the model card from the record

A model card written by hand drifts from the truth the first time someone retrains without updating it. Generate the factual parts from the record, and keep only the judgment (intended use, limitations) hand-written:

MODEL_CARD.md sits inside the version folder, so it's versioned with the artifact. Writing it doesn't break immutability: the record and the artifact are the parts that never change, and the hash check covers the artifact.

#Step 8: The same registry in MLflow

Every function you wrote has an MLflow equivalent, so moving to a shared server later changes the calls, not the ideas:

This lesson MLflow (3.x)
register(model, name, version, ...) mlflow.sklearn.log_model(sk_model=model, name="model", registered_model_name=name) inside a run
record.json params and metrics mlflow.log_params(...), mlflow.log_metrics(...)
training_data hashes mlflow.log_input(mlflow.data.from_pandas(...), context="training"), plus a data_sha256 tag if you want the file hash
Semantic version string MLflow's integer version, with client.set_model_version_tag(name, version, "semver", "1.1.0")
set_alias(name, "champion", version) client.set_registered_model_alias(name, "champion", version)
load_alias(name, "champion") mlflow.sklearn.load_model("models:/late-delivery@champion")
aliases.json history Not kept by MLflow automatically; record moves in tags or your deploy log

That last row is a real difference worth knowing: a registry service tells you where an alias points now, and you may still need your own record of where it pointed then.

#The finished registry

Commit registry/ while the artifacts are small. When they grow to many megabytes, keep the records and aliases in Git and move the model.joblib files to object storage (an S3-compatible bucket, for example), still addressed by version and still checked against the recorded hash.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does register() raise instead of overwriting when a version already exists?

  • The point isn't space; it's that a version number must always mean the same bytes.

  • Immutability is what lets an incident review trust "1.1.0 was serving". A fix gets a new version number.

  • joblib overwrites files without complaint; the check exists because it would.

Show answer

B. Immutability is what lets an incident review trust "1.1.0 was serving". A fix gets a new version number.

2Why does load_alias hash the artifact before calling joblib.load?

  • Order doesn't affect hashing speed; it affects what runs first.

  • Checking first catches corruption and tampering before the file is ever opened as a model.

  • The record stores the hash of the file's bytes, written right after joblib.dump.

Show answer

B. Checking first catches corruption and tampering before the file is ever opened as a model.

31.1.0 is champion and misbehaving. What does rollback() change on disk?

  • Deleting it would destroy the evidence you need to investigate, and the version could never be reproduced.

  • Only aliases.json changes. Both version folders stay exactly as registered.

  • Unnecessary: 1.0.0's artifact is still in the registry, and its hash proves it's unchanged.

Show answer

B. Only aliases.json changes. Both version folders stay exactly as registered.

Key takeaways

  • A version is a folder that is written once: artifact, record, and (optionally) a model card.
  • Records hash every training file and the artifact, and name the parent version.
  • Aliases move; their history is appended, never edited, so rollback is one recorded move.
  • Promotion goes through a written gate on a fixed holdout; registering is not deploying.
  • Verify the artifact's hash before unpickling, and expose version and hash on /health.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a challenger alias and have the service score each request with both models, returning only the champion's answer and logging the challenger's for comparison (called shadow deployment).
  • Pass the version into the Docker build with ARG MODEL_VERSION and COPY registry/late-delivery/${MODEL_VERSION}/ models/, and tag the image with the same version.
  • Make register() record git_commit() from the Notes lesson, and refuse to register from a -dirty working tree.

#Further reading

  • MLflow: Model Registry workflows (opens in a new tab): registering, aliasing, tagging, and loading models with the client API.
  • Hugging Face: Model Cards (opens in a new tab): a widely used card format, with the metadata fields Hugging Face reads.

m4-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Decide MAJOR, MINOR, PATCH, or no model version for realistic changes.
  • Build a dataset fingerprint that ignores row and column order but catches any changed value.
  • Audit a registry record by re-hashing its artifact and training files.
  • Answer lineage questions: which versions used a bad file, and which alias served at a given time.
  • Write a promotion gate with several rules, and a function that proposes the next version number.

#Warm-up: which bump?

Using the convention from the Notes lesson (MAJOR = the request or response contract changes, MINOR = same contract but outputs change, PATCH = outputs identical), decide each case. One of them isn't a new model version at all.

  1. Retrain on March's orders with the same features and code.
  2. Add a required restaurant_id field to the request.
  3. Fix a misspelled word in the record's params description; the artifact is untouched.
  4. Lower the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.45.
  5. Rename the response field late_probability to p_late.
  6. Rebuild the Docker image because the python:3.12-slim base image got a security patch; model.joblib is byte-identical.
Show solution
  1. MINOR. Same contract, new weights, so some outputs change.
  2. MAJOR. Every client must start sending a new field.
  3. PATCH. Nothing any client can observe changed. (Some teams skip a version entirely for this; a PATCH keeps the record immutable.)
  4. MINOR. The response has the same fields, but late flips for some orders.
  5. MAJOR. Renaming a response field breaks every client that reads it, even though the numbers are the same.
  6. No new model version. The model didn't change; the image did. It gets a new image digest (and usually a new image tag such as 1.1.0-2), while the registry record for 1.1.0 stays as it is. Keeping model versions and image builds separate is what lets you patch the OS without re-validating the model.

#Setup

#Exercise 1: A fingerprint that ignores order

The file hash changes when rows are shuffled, even though the data is the same. Write dataset_fingerprint(frame) that returns the same SHA-256 for the same set of rows and columns in any order, and a different one if any value changes. Check it on four frames: the original, shuffled rows, reordered columns, and one value edited.

Need a hint?

Put the frame in a canonical form first: columns in sorted order, then rows sorted by every column, then a fresh index. pd.util.hash_pandas_object(frame, index=False) gives one 64-bit hash per row; hash the bytes of that array with SHA-256.

Show solution

The column names go into the hash too; otherwise renaming items to basket_size would leave the fingerprint unchanged. Which hash should a registry record use? Both answer different questions. The file hash says "these exact bytes", which is what reproducing a training run needs (the Notes lesson showed that row order changes the artifact's bytes slightly). The fingerprint says "the same data", which is what you want when comparing exports from two systems.

#Exercise 2: Audit a record against the disk

A registry record claims a data hash and an artifact hash. Write audit(record) that re-hashes the artifact and every training file and returns a list of problems (an empty list means the record checks out). Then append one row to the training file and audit again.

Need a hint?

Loop over record["training_data"]. Use Path(...).exists() before hashing, so a missing file is reported as a problem instead of crashing the audit.

Show solution

An audit like this is cheap enough to run in CI on every commit. It catches the quiet failure where someone "fixes" a training file in place, and every record that points at it silently stops being reproducible.

#Exercise 3: Which versions used the bad file?

The data team reports that orders_2026_02.csv with hash e0b9e96a... had labels shifted by one row. Given these registry records and the current aliases, list every version trained on that file, and say whether any alias points at one of them right now.

Need a hint?

Match on the hash, not the file name. Version 1.2.0 was trained on a file with the same name but different contents.

Show solution

Matching by name would have flagged 1.2.0 too, and the team would have rolled back their only clean candidate. Names say where a file lives; hashes say what's in it. The answer also tells you what to do: the champion is affected, 1.0.0 is the most recent unaffected version with a record, so the fast fix is to roll champion back to 1.0.0 while 1.2.0 finishes evaluation.

#Exercise 4: What was serving at 14:05?

An incident started at 14:05 on 17 November. Write alias_at(history, alias, when) that returns which version an alias pointed to at a given moment, using the append-only history from the Build-along. Test it at four times, including one before the alias existed.

Need a hint?

Walk the moves in time order and remember the latest move for this alias that happened at or before when. Compare times as datetime objects with datetime.fromisoformat, not as strings.

Show solution

This is the question from the Notes lesson's incident report, answered in one line. It only works because the history is append-only: if set_alias had simply overwritten current, 14:05 would be unanswerable. (Comparing ISO strings happens to work when every timestamp has the same format and time zone; converting to datetime stays correct when they don't.)

#Exercise 5: A promotion gate with several rules

Write gate(candidate, champion, serving_sklearn) returning a list of reasons to refuse promotion. Refuse if:

  • the holdout AUC drops by more than 0.002,
  • the feature list changed but the MAJOR number didn't go up,
  • the candidate was built with a different scikit-learn than the serving image has,
  • the candidate has no model card.

Test it on the three candidates below.

Need a hint?

int(version.split(".")[0]) gives the MAJOR number. Collect every problem rather than returning at the first one: a person fixing a candidate wants the whole list at once.

Show solution

The second candidate is the interesting one: it's the best model by far, and the gate still refuses it. A new required feature means every client must change, so it has to ship as 2.0.0 with a new contract, a migration plan, and probably both versions served side by side for a while. A gate that only looked at metrics would have broken every client at once.

#Exercise 6: Does this environment match the record?

A record lists the library versions the model was trained with. Write environment_mismatches(recorded) that compares them with what's installed right now (using importlib.metadata.version) and lists every difference, including packages that aren't installed. Test it with a record that has one stale version and one package this machine lacks.

Need a hint?

installed_version("scikit-learn") returns a string such as "1.8.0". It raises PackageNotFoundError for a package that isn't installed. Use distribution names as pip knows them (scikit-learn, not sklearn).

Show solution

Run this at service startup (like the Module 2 challenge did for scikit-learn alone) or as a CI step that compares the training record with the serving image's requirements.txt. Either way, a mismatch becomes a clear message instead of a silent change in predictions.

#Challenge: Propose the next version automatically

Write next_version(champion, candidate) that compares two records and proposes the candidate's version number from the champion's: MAJOR if the features or the response fields differ, MINOR if the artifact hash or the threshold differs, otherwise PATCH. Write unit tests for each case and run them so the results print.

Need a hint?

Parse "1.4.2" into three integers. A MAJOR bump resets MINOR and PATCH to zero (1.4.2 becomes 2.0.0), and a MINOR bump resets PATCH (1.4.2 becomes 1.5.0). Build the test records with a helper that starts from a base record and overrides one field.

Show solution

The order of the checks encodes the priority: a contract change outranks everything else. A tool like this belongs in the training pipeline, which can then refuse to register a candidate whose hand-typed version disagrees with the proposal. That turns the convention from something people remember into something the pipeline enforces.

What you'll learn

  • Order a training pipeline so a failed check stops every step after it, including publishing.
  • Write unit tests for feature code and data tests for a batch's schema and value ranges.
  • Turn a model metric into a quality gate that compares against a floor and the current champion.
  • Explain what a GitHub Actions workflow does with those tests every time you push.

This is the log from the nightly training job for the late-delivery model, the one that warns customers when their food will probably arrive late:

Nothing crashed, and the evaluation step did its job: it caught a model that was no better than a coin flip. It just ran fourth, after the publish step had pushed 1.4.0 and the deploy hook had picked it up. For eleven hours the app told customers their orders were on time based on a model that had learned nothing. The fix isn't a smarter test. It's moving the test in front of the door.

#Each step has to earn the next one

Think of an assembly line with inspectors. A part that fails inspection never reaches the shipping dock, because the dock is at the end and the line stops when an inspector says no.

Precisely: a training pipeline is a set of steps where each one reads artifacts from earlier steps and writes new ones (a cleaned dataset, a model file, a metrics report). Two rules keep it safe. Every check runs before the step it protects. And any failure stops everything downstream, so the steps with side effects that leave the pipeline, like publishing to a registry or deploying, sit at the very end.

A pipeline runner can be tiny. Step through this one and watch what happens to published when the data check fails on the second row:

The break is the entire safety mechanism. train and publish never run, so published stays None. Real orchestrators give you the same guarantee by default: in Airflow a task whose upstream task failed is marked upstream_failed and skipped, and in GitHub Actions a job that needs: a failed job is skipped. Your job is to put the steps in the right order.

#Four kinds of tests an ML repo needs

Ordinary software has unit tests. ML code needs those plus tests for the two things that change without anyone editing code: the data and the model.

Test What it protects Example check When it runs
Unit Feature and helper code rush_hour is 1 at 19:00 and 0 at 20:00 every push, milliseconds
Data The batch you are about to train or score on no missing columns, hour in 0–23 every pipeline run
Model The trained model ROC AUC ≥ 0.75 and not worse than the champion after training
Service The API contract /predict returns a probability in [0, 1]; bad input gets 422 every push

Here is make_orders from the make_data.py you wrote in Module 2, which rebuilds data/orders.csv. Lateness is built in from distance, item count, rain, and the 17:00–19:59 dinner rush, so you know what a working model should find.

Unit tests come first because they're the cheapest. Feature code is where off-by-one bugs hide. Suppose you add an explicit rush_hour column: does the rush include 7 p.m.? Pin the answer down in a test so nobody changes it by accident.

Tests here are written pytest-style, as plain functions named test_... that use assert. On this page, a small run_tests helper wraps each function in unittest.FunctionTestCase and prints the results; in the repo, python -m pytest finds the same functions by their names.

Each test function is one claim about the code. The message after the comma in an assert is printed when it fails; pytest adds its own detailed diff on top, but a plain message keeps the failure readable anywhere.

🧪 Try it yourself

Change between(17, 19) to between(17, 20) in add_features and run the cell again. test_rush_hour_boundaries fails with AssertionError: rush_hour for 16, 17, 19, 20 was [0, 1, 1, 1], pointing at the exact hour that moved.

#Data tests: check the batch before you trust it

Code changes go through review. Data doesn't. An upstream team renames a column, a timezone conversion produces hour 24, a GPS bug reports negative distances, and none of it shows up in your git history. A data test states what a valid batch looks like and lists every way the current batch breaks the rule.

Notice that validate collects every problem instead of stopping at the first. When a 2 a.m. job fails, the person reading the log wants the whole list, not one problem per rerun. The late-rate check is a range rather than an exact value: lateness drifts a little with weather and season, but a jump to 95% means the labels are broken.

#A quality gate turns a metric into pass or fail

A metric printed in a log is a suggestion. A quality gate is a rule that fails the pipeline. A useful gate checks two things: an absolute floor (below this, the model isn't fit for the job) and a comparison with the champion, the model in production now (a new model shouldn't be noticeably worse than what it replaces).

The pipeline below is build_pipeline() from your train.py, unchanged:

The broken model trained without complaint. Shuffled labels produce a perfectly valid model file; it just learned noise. Only the gate notices. In CI the gate is a script that ends with sys.exit(1 if failures else 0). The exit code is the contract: the runner treats any non-zero exit as a failed step.

Pick the gate's metric carefully. Here is the most common gate bug for any model where one class is rare:

A model that predicts "on time" for every order scores about 0.70 accuracy without looking at a single feature, because roughly 70% of orders are on time. A gate of "accuracy ≥ 0.65" would wave it through. AUC sits at exactly 0.5 for a model whose scores carry no ranking information, so it can't be fooled that way.

#CI runs the same checks on every push

Continuous integration means every change is tested automatically before it's merged. On GitHub, you describe the checks in a YAML file under .github/workflows/. On each push or pull request, GitHub starts a fresh virtual machine (a runner), checks out your code, and runs your steps in order. If any step exits non-zero, the job fails, later steps are skipped, and the pull request shows a red X.

A minimal workflow looks like this. You'll build the full version next lesson.

A red X only informs people. To make it block merging, a repository admin turns on branch protection (or a ruleset) for main with "Require status checks to pass before merging" and selects the test job.

⚠️ Watch out

Three gates that look fine and aren't.

  1. Accuracy on imbalanced data. As the lazy model showed, "always say no" passes an accuracy gate. Gate on AUC, recall at a fixed threshold, or precision, whichever matches the cost of a mistake.
  2. Randomness without seeds. Leave out random_state and the same code passes on Monday and fails on Tuesday. A flaky gate teaches the team to click "re-run" until it's green. Seed the split and the model, and leave a margin between typical scores and the threshold.
  3. Paths from your laptop. pd.read_csv("C:/Users/sam/data.csv") passes locally and fails on the runner with FileNotFoundError. Every file a test reads must be in the repo or created by an earlier step.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A pipeline runs validate → train → publish → evaluate, and evaluate fails. What is in the registry afterward?

  • The run failed, but publish had already succeeded before evaluate ran. Failure only stops the steps after it.

  • Publish ran third and succeeded. The failing evaluation came too late to stop it, which is exactly the bug in the opening log.

  • Nothing in this pipeline restores anything. Rollback is a separate action you'd have to build.

Show answer

B. Publish ran third and succeeded. The failing evaluation came too late to stop it, which is exactly the bug in the opening log.

230% of orders are late. Your gate requires accuracy ≥ 0.65. Which model passes?

  • A model that predicts "on time" for everything scores about 0.70 accuracy and passes too.

  • Accuracy rewards the majority class. The lazy model's AUC of 0.5 would expose it, but this gate doesn't check AUC.

  • The lazy model reaches about 0.70 just by matching the majority.

Show answer

B. Accuracy rewards the majority class. The lazy model's AUC of 0.5 would expose it, but this gate doesn't check AUC.

3Why compare the candidate with the champion as well as with a fixed floor?

  • A floor of 0.75 lets a 0.76 model replace a 0.81 one. The champion comparison stops that regression.

  • Both numbers come from evaluation data. The comparison is about not getting worse, not about which number is truer.

  • Registries store whatever you send them. Enforcing the comparison is the gate's job.

Show answer

A. A floor of 0.75 lets a 0.76 model replace a 0.81 one. The champion comparison stops that regression.

4In a GitHub Actions job, python gate.py exits with code 1. What happens to the upload-artifact step listed after it?

  • By default, a failed step stops the job, and later steps are skipped.

  • Steps run in order and stop at the first non-zero exit unless a step opts in with if: always().

  • Actions doesn't retry steps on its own. Someone would have to re-run the job.

Show answer

B. Steps run in order and stop at the first non-zero exit unless a step opts in with if: always().

Key takeaways

  • Put every check before the step it protects, and put publishing and deploying last.
  • ML repos need four kinds of tests: unit tests for code, data tests for batches, quality gates for models, and contract tests for the API.
  • A data test should report every problem it finds, with counts, so one failed run tells the whole story.
  • A gate is a script that exits non-zero. Gate on a metric the lazy model can't game, and compare against both a floor and the champion.
  • CI runs on a clean machine for every push, so tests can only depend on what's in the repo.

#Further reading

  • Understanding GitHub Actions (opens in a new tab): the official overview of workflows, events, jobs, runners, and steps.
  • The ML Test Score (opens in a new tab): Google's checklist of 28 tests for production ML, grouped into data, model, infrastructure, and monitoring.
  • MLOps: continuous delivery and automation pipelines in ML (opens in a new tab): how pipeline automation grows from manual notebooks to full CI/CD, with diagrams of each level.

What you'll learn

  • Write pytest-style data tests that read the training file and explain each failure in their message.
  • Write behavioral model tests and a gate.py that exits 1 when a candidate is worse than the floor or the champion.
  • Pin the API's request and response schema with a snapshot test, so a renamed field fails CI.
  • Assemble a GitHub Actions workflow whose step order guarantees a bad model is never uploaded.

By the end of this build, pushing a broken model to the late-delivery repo produces a red X instead of a deploy. You already have make_data.py, train.py, app/main.py, and tests/test_api.py from Module 2. This lesson adds the files marked "new":

Each cell below is one file in the repo. On this page the cells run in order, and later cells read the files earlier cells write.

#Step 1: Rebuild the data and make training traceable

This first cell is your make_data.py plus the small run_tests helper from the Notes lesson, which prints pytest-style test results on this page. In the repo, python -m pytest does that job.

train.py is the Module 2 script with two changes. main() now takes the CSV path, so CI can point it at any export. And model.json records the commit the model was built from and a hash of its training data, the same traceability your Module 4 registry records insist on.

GITHUB_SHA is set automatically on every Actions runner to the commit being tested, so a model built in CI can be traced to the exact code that made it. On your laptop it falls back to "local". The data hash changes if even one byte of the CSV changes, so "was this model trained on the file I think it was?" has a yes-or-no answer.

#Step 2: Data tests that explain themselves

Each test checks one property of the file. The assert message is what a tired person reads at 2 a.m., so put the count and an example of the bad value in it. A bare assert bad.empty fails with nothing but AssertionError.

All seven pass on the good file. Now feed them what a timezone bug upstream would produce:

One F among the dots, and the failure names the problem and an example value. Because every test calls load(), which reads DATA_PATH when it runs, pointing that variable at another file is all it takes to test a different export.

#Step 3: Model tests and the gate

Metrics say how good the model is on average. Behavioral tests check specific things you know must be true, the way you'd sanity-check a new teammate's work. If a 12 km order in the rain scores less likely to be late than a 2 km order on a dry afternoon, something is wrong even if AUC looks fine. These tests load the candidate that train.py just saved:

Now the gate. A fair comparison scores both models on the same rows, so it uses the frozen data/holdout.csv and loads the champion the way your Module 4 service does: look up the champion alias, then check the artifact's hash against its record before unpickling. This cell sets up a minimal copy of that registry, with 1.0.0 as champion:

The gate prints a side-by-side table and returns an exit code. The real file ends with sys.exit(gate()); here the code is printed so you can see it.

Retrained on the same data, the candidate is the champion, so the two columns match exactly, which is a useful check in itself: training is reproducible. Recall is the share of late orders that got a warning; warn rate is how often any customer sees one. The warn-rate rule is a product decision, not a statistics one. A model that warns on half of all orders might catch nearly every late one, but customers would learn to ignore the warning. Gates are where those constraints get written down.

To see the gate earn its keep, simulate a broken label join: same rows, labels shuffled. The data tests can't see it, because every column is still valid.

Data tests pass and the gate fails. That's why you need both layers: each catches failures the other can't see.

#Step 4: Pin the API contract with a snapshot

tests/test_api.py from Module 2 already checks status codes and value ranges. One gap remains: nothing notices if someone renames a response field and updates the tests to match. The mobile app, which nobody re-tested, breaks in production. A snapshot test saves the request and response schemas once, commits them, and fails whenever the live schema differs.

This is the Module 2 service, unchanged:

FastAPI already describes both models in the OpenAPI document it serves at /openapi.json. The test reduces that to the part callers depend on: each field's name and type, and which fields are required.

Now play the teammate who "tidies up" the response by renaming late_probability to probability:

The failure tells the reviewer exactly what changed for callers. The snapshot doesn't forbid change; it forces the change to be deliberate, with a regenerated snapshot showing up in the pull request's diff where someone can ask "did we tell the mobile team?"

#Step 5: The workflow file

Now wire it together. Two jobs: lint is fast and runs first, and test waits for it with needs: lint. Inside test, the step order is the pipeline from the diagram at the top.

cache: pip tells setup-python to cache downloaded packages, keyed on a hash of the files matched by cache-dependency-path. Matching both requirements files means a change to either one refreshes the cache. python -m pytest rather than bare pytest keeps the project root on the import path, so from app.main import app works on the runner just as it does on your laptop. In tests/test_contract.py, delete the two snapshot-writing lines at the bottom once the snapshot is committed, or CI will overwrite the snapshot instead of checking it.

When the gate fails on a runner, the step log ends like this, and the upload step shows as skipped:

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the workflow run the data tests before training instead of after?

  • A failing data test names the actual problem in seconds. Training first could produce a bad model whose gate failure hides the real cause.

  • Steps run in whatever order you list them. The order is a design decision.

  • It's the reverse: data tests read only the CSV, while model tests need the artifact.

Show answer

A. A failing data test names the actual problem in seconds. Training first could produce a bad model whose gate failure hides the real cause.

2The shuffled-label file passed every data test. What does that tell you?

  • They caught the timezone bug, which the gate might have missed. Each layer catches failures the other can't.

  • Every value was individually valid; only the relationship between features and labels was broken. The gate measures that relationship.

  • A join on the wrong key, or a sort applied to one column but not another, does exactly this.

Show answer

B. Every value was individually valid; only the relationship between features and labels was broken. The gate measures that relationship.

3A teammate moves the upload step to just after "Train candidate" so artifacts are available for debugging. What's the risk?

  • The gate still runs, but the artifact already exists by then. Anything that consumes uploaded artifacts can pick up a failing model.

  • To keep failing models for debugging, upload them under a different name in a separate step with if: failure().

  • It doesn't refuse. Uploads that finished before the failure are kept.

Show answer

B. To keep failing models for debugging, upload them under a different name in a separate step with if: failure().

Key takeaways

  • train.py writes a model file and traceable metadata, and every later check loads those artifacts instead of retraining.
  • Assert messages are documentation. Put the count and an example of the bad value in them.
  • Behavioral tests check things you know must be true, such as "rain never lowers the risk of lateness," which an average metric can hide.
  • gate.py holds both statistical rules (floors, champion comparison) and product rules (how often customers see a warning).
  • A committed schema snapshot turns a silent breaking change for callers into a failed test and a visible diff.
  • In the workflow, step order is the safety guarantee. Upload last.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a second upload step with if: failure() named rejected-model-${{ github.sha }}, so failed candidates can be inspected without being mistaken for good ones.
  • Write the gate's table to the job summary by appending Markdown to the file named in the GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY environment variable, so reviewers see the metrics on the run page.
  • Add a schedule: trigger with a cron: expression to retrain nightly on fresh data, behind the same gates.

#Further reading

  • Building and testing Python (opens in a new tab): GitHub's guide to setup-python, dependency caching, and test matrices.
  • FastAPI: Testing (opens in a new tab): how TestClient works, including testing apps split across files.
  • Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions (opens in a new tab): the reference for on, needs, if, and every other key used above.

What you'll learn

  • Catch a unit change that every range check misses by comparing a batch with reference statistics.
  • Run pipeline steps from declared dependencies so a failure skips everything downstream.
  • Gate a candidate per slice, not just overall, and pick a floor that random noise can't trip.
  • Write API tests and workflow conditions that fail for the right reasons.

Every exercise uses the late-delivery orders and the champion model (version 1.0.0) from your train.py. Run this cell first; later cells build on it.

#Warm-up: which layer catches it?

For each bug, name the first test layer (unit, data, model gate, or API contract) that would fail:

  1. A new rush_hour helper treats 20:00 as rush hour.
  2. The export has 300 rows where hour is missing.
  3. A refactor makes /predict return {"probability": 0.4, ...}.
  4. Labels were joined on the wrong key, so every value is valid but late is random.
Show solution
  1. Unit: a boundary test on rush_hour pins 19 → 1 and 20 → 0.
  2. Data: the no-missing-values test fails before training starts.
  3. API contract: both the Module 2 response tests and the schema snapshot expect late_probability.
  4. Model gate: every value passes the data tests, but AUC falls to about 0.5. Only a test of what the model learned can see a broken relationship between columns.

#Exercise 1: Catch a unit change that passes every range check

The partner app's new release reports distance_km in miles. Every value is still between 0 and 50, so the range test passes. Write compare_to_reference(batch, reference, cols, tolerance=0.25) that prints each column's median next to the reference median and flags any that moved by more than 25%.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Compute batch[col].median() / reference[col].median() - 1 for each column. Leave binary columns like raining out; their median is usually 0, and you can't divide by it.

Show solution

A median is robust to a few outliers, so a 500-row batch from the same source usually lands within about 10% of the reference, while a units change moves the whole distribution at once. The tolerance is a judgment call: tight enough to catch miles (−37%), loose enough that ordinary batch-to-batch variation doesn't page anyone. Module 6 turns this idea into proper drift statistics.

#Exercise 2: Fix a pipeline that publishes after a failure

This runner has the two bugs from the incident at the start of the module: the steps are listed in the wrong order, and a failed step doesn't stop the ones after it.

Rewrite it as run_dag(steps), where each step declares what it needs, like {"publish": (publish, ["gate"])}. The runner works out the order itself and skips any step whose dependencies didn't succeed. Sample output, even when the dict lists publish first:

Need a hint?

The standard library has a topological sorter: graphlib.TopologicalSorter(graph).static_order() takes {node: [dependencies]} and yields nodes so that every dependency comes first. Keep a status dict and check it before running each step.

Show solution

Declaring dependencies instead of a list order removes a whole class of bug: nobody can "tidy up" the step list and accidentally move publishing earlier. A skipped step counts as not-ok, so a failure cascades all the way down the graph. Airflow DAGs and GitHub Actions needs: work on the same model.

#Exercise 3: A gate that checks every slice

A teammate "simplified" the pipeline: instead of one-hot encoding hour, it now just scales it like the other numbers. Overall AUC went up. Write slice_gate(champion, candidate, val, max_drop=0.05) that computes recall at the 0.5 threshold on five slices (all orders, rainy, dry, the 17:00–19:59 rush, and orders over 6 km) and fails any slice where the candidate's recall drops by more than 0.05.

The gate from this module's build would pass the candidate without a second look. Sample output of your slice gate:

Need a hint?

Define slices as boolean masks over val_df, for example {"rainy": (val_df.raining == 1).to_numpy()}. Score both models once, then index the predictions with each mask before calling recall_score(y[mask], warned[mask]).

Show solution

A single scaled hour column can only say "later is riskier" or "later is safer"; it can't say "17:00 to 19:59 is special." So the candidate lost over a third of its warnings for dinner-rush customers, the people most likely to be late, while its ranking elsewhere improved enough to lift overall AUC. An average over everyone can hide a group that got much worse. Choose slices from how the product is used (weather, time of day, distance, city) and check that each has enough validation rows to give a stable number: the rush slice here has about a hundred.

#Exercise 4: A contract test that catches the wrong column

This service passes a field-name test and a 0-to-1 range test, yet it's badly broken. Write tests that fail on it, then fix the app.

Need a hint?

predict_proba returns one column per class, in the order of model.classes_, which is [0, 1] here. Column 0 is the probability of being on time. A test can't know the exact right number, but it does know that a 12 km order in the rain at dinner rush must score higher than a 1.5 km dry order before lunch.

Show solution

The range test passes on the buggy app because 1 − p is also between 0 and 1. The ordering test is a behavioral check through the API, and it catches any bug that inverts or scrambles scores. Pairs of known-safe and known-risky inputs make good API tests because they don't depend on exact model numbers, so they keep passing every time you retrain.

#Exercise 5: Pick a floor that randomness can't trip

A teammate set the gate's AUC floor to 0.80 because "that's what the last run got," and train_test_split has no fixed random_state. Simulate 20 unseeded CI runs by training with split seeds 0 to 19, count how many would fail a 0.80 floor, and propose a better policy.

Sample output:

Need a hint?

Loop over range(20), call train_test_split(..., random_state=seed), fit build_pipeline(), and store each validation AUC in a list. np.mean, np.std, and a comparison like (aucs < 0.80).sum() give the summary.

Show solution

Roughly half the runs fail with no change to the code at all. That's a coin flip wearing a gate's uniform, and teams respond by re-running until it's green, which is worse than having no gate. The fix has two parts. Fix the seed (random_state=0, as train.py already does) so the same commit always gives the same number. Then put the floor below the noise band (here about 0.73), so it fires on real regressions and never on lucky splits.

Notice how wide that band is: with 500 validation rows, AUC wobbles by about ±0.02 between splits. A gate can't reliably detect a 0.01 regression on that much data. Either validate on more rows, or compare the two models on the same rows, which is what the challenge does.

#Exercise 6: Deploy only from main, only after tests pass

Add a deploy job to the workflow from this module's build. It must run only after test succeeds, only for pushes to main (never for pull requests), and it needs the model artifact that test uploaded. Deployment itself can be a placeholder run: line for now.

Need a hint?

needs: test handles ordering and success. For the branch, an if: on the job can check github.event_name and github.ref; a push to main has github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'. The matching action for fetching artifacts is actions/download-artifact.

Show solution

needs: test means the job is skipped whenever test fails, so no extra check for gate success is required. On a pull request, github.event_name is pull_request, so the if: is false and the job shows as skipped. environment: production is optional but useful: in the repository's settings you can attach protection rules to an environment, such as required reviewers, so a person approves each deploy.

#Challenge: Is the improvement real?

Exercise 3's simplified candidate beat the champion's AUC by about 0.017. On 500 validation rows, is that a real improvement or a lucky sample? Write a paired bootstrap: resample validation rows with replacement 500 times, compute candidate AUC minus champion AUC on the same resample each time, and report the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Then decide what the overall gate (lower bound above −0.01) and the slice gate would each say. Hint: score both models once, then resample index arrays with rng.integers(0, n, n).

Show solution

Pairing matters. Both models are scored on the same resampled rows, so row-to-row difficulty cancels out and the interval is much narrower than two separate intervals would be. The interval includes zero, so you can't claim the candidate is better, only that it probably isn't more than 0.01 worse overall. The overall gate passes it; the slice gate from Exercise 3 still rejects it for dinner-rush customers. Production gates usually need both kinds of check.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Explain the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment, and why you build one immutable image per commit.
  • Compare recreate, rolling, blue-green, canary, and shadow releases by what users see when the new version is bad.
  • Write separate liveness and readiness checks, where readiness proves the right model is loaded and working.
  • Monitor the four golden signals plus input drift, and write alert rules that wait for a sustained breach.

Model 1.1.0 of the late-delivery service passed every gate from Module 5. Its AUC was 0.01 higher than 1.0.0's, the data tests were green, and the contract snapshot matched. Ten minutes after it went live, the dashboard looked like this:

Offline tests measure what a model predicts. They don't measure how long it takes under real traffic, or what happens with inputs nobody put in the validation set. In this case the new model loaded a larger lookup table lazily, so about one request in twenty paid the loading cost, and orders from a newly launched zone hit a code path that crashed. The median didn't budge, which is why nobody noticed in the first minute. This module is about the two things that would have contained it: releasing gradually, and watching the right numbers.

#From "tests pass" to "it's live"

Continuous delivery means every commit that passes CI produces a release you could deploy with one click. Continuous deployment goes one step further: it deploys automatically. Either way, two rules make it safe.

First, build once, deploy that artifact everywhere. The Docker image is built from one commit, tagged with that commit's SHA, and never rebuilt for staging or production. If staging tested image sha-3f9c2e1, production runs sha-3f9c2e1, byte for byte. Rebuilding "the same code" later can pull different base-image patches or package versions.

Second, verify after deploying. A deploy isn't done when the platform says "live"; it's done when the new version answers correctly.

Render, where you deployed in Module 3, gives each service a secret deploy hook URL on its Settings page; a GET or POST to it starts a deploy, and adding ref=<commit SHA> deploys that exact commit. Store the URL as a repository secret and add a job after test:

The deploy hook URL already contains ?key=..., which is why ref is appended with &. If you'd rather not write a job at all, Render's Auto-Deploy setting has an After CI Checks Pass option that waits for your checks before deploying each push to the linked branch. Either way, Render's zero-downtime deploys keep the old instance serving until the new one passes its health check, and cancel the deploy if it never does.

#Five ways to switch versions

How you move traffic from 1.0.0 to 1.1.0 decides how many users meet a bad release, and how fast you can undo it.

Strategy How it works If 1.1.0 is bad Extra cost
Recreate Stop old, start new Everyone, plus downtime None
Rolling Replace instances a few at a time A growing share during the roll Little
Blue-green Start a full new copy, switch all traffic at once Everyone, but switching back is instant Double capacity briefly
Canary Send a small share (say 5%) to the new version, widen in steps Only the canary share, until you stop Little
Shadow Copy requests to the new version, ignore its answers Nobody; you only compare Double compute

Shadow is unusually useful for ML: the new model scores real traffic and you compare its predictions and latency with the champion's, at zero risk to users. You can't measure user-facing effects that way, which is what a canary is for. Render's own deploys are blue-green style. Weighted canaries need a platform that splits traffic (Cloud Run does it with gcloud run services update-traffic SERVICE --to-revisions REVISION=5, and Kubernetes tools such as Argo Rollouts do it too) or a small router of your own.

A router has to make one decision: which version serves this request? Hash a stable ID rather than flipping a coin, so each customer stays on the same version across requests:

The hash maps each ID to one of 10,000 buckets, and the canary owns buckets below the threshold. Because widening only raises the threshold, everyone already on the canary stays there. That stickiness matters: a customer whose ETA warning flips between models on every refresh would rightly lose trust in it.

#Health checks that know about the model

Platforms ask two different questions, and they deserve two endpoints. Liveness asks "is the process stuck?" A failed liveness check gets the container restarted. Readiness asks "should this instance receive traffic right now?" A failed readiness check takes the instance out of rotation without killing it. In Kubernetes these are the livenessProbe and readinessProbe; Render's health check path and Docker's HEALTHCHECK each use one endpoint, so point them at readiness.

Your Module 2 /health returns 503 until the model is loaded, which is a good start. A model-aware readiness check goes further: is this the version the deploy expected, and does it still give the answer it gave at training time for a fixed golden order?

The golden check costs one prediction and catches failures nothing else does: a model file saved by a different scikit-learn that loads but scores differently, or preprocessing that changed between training and serving. The version check catches a deploy that silently kept the old artifact. Keep liveness trivial, though. If /livez checked the model too, a slow model load would get the container restarted in a loop, and it would never finish starting.

#What to watch, and when to wake someone

Google's SRE book names four golden signals for any service: latency (how long requests take), traffic (how many arrive), errors (how many fail), and saturation (how full the service is: CPU, memory, queue length). An ML service adds three of its own: the distribution of inputs, the distribution of predictions, and, once outcomes arrive, accuracy. For this service the outcome is cheap to get: within an hour you know whether each order was actually late.

All of that comes from one structured log line per prediction, written by the service and shipped to whatever log store you use:

Here are an hour of those lines for the opening incident, with 1.1.0 deployed at minute 30, summarized per minute:

A dashboard is for humans who are already looking. An alert is for when nobody is. Two rules keep alerts trustworthy. Alert on symptoms users feel (slow responses, errors) rather than on causes (CPU at 80%), since a busy CPU that hurts no one shouldn't wake anyone. And require the breach to last, because single bad minutes happen all the time. Step through a rule that pages only after three consecutive minutes with p99 above 300 ms:

The lone spike at minute 2 resets to zero a minute later and never pages. The real regression pages at minute 7, two minutes after it started. That delay is the price of not paging on noise, and you tune it per alert: a few minutes for "users are failing," hours for "this input looks a bit unusual."

#Drift: when the world stops matching the training data

A model learns the relationship between inputs and outcomes from one slice of history. Two things can change afterward:

  • Data drift: the inputs change. The company launches in a suburban zone, and distances get longer. The model may still be right about each order, but it's now working in a region it saw little of.
  • Concept drift: the relationship changes. A bridge closes, and the same 5 km now takes twice as long. Inputs look exactly as before; the model is simply wrong.

Data drift shows up immediately in the prediction log. Concept drift only shows up when outcomes arrive, as a drop in accuracy. Two standard ways to compare a feature's live distribution with its training distribution:

PSI (population stability index) bins the reference data into, say, 10 equal-count buckets, measures what fraction of each sample lands in each bucket, and adds up (a - e) * ln(a / e) over the buckets, where e is a bucket's expected (reference) fraction and a its actual (live) one. A common rule of thumb from credit scoring: below 0.1 is stable, 0.1 to 0.25 is worth a look, above 0.25 is a real shift. The Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) test measures the largest vertical gap between the two cumulative distributions; scipy.stats.ks_2samp returns that gap and a p-value.

Distance drifts and the other features don't, which is exactly the story: same customers and menus, new geography. The KS p-value for distance is astronomically small. Don't read that as "very important": with thousands of rows, even a trivial shift gets a tiny p-value. Judge size with the statistic itself (PSI, or the KS gap), and use the p-value only to rule out noise on small samples. You'll compute all of this from a real prediction log in the next lesson.

⚠️ Watch out

Three monitoring mistakes that bite in the first month.

  1. Alerting on the mean. In the chart above, mean latency roughly tripled while p99 grew more than twentyfold. Alert on the percentile in your objective, not on the average.
  2. One noisy minute, one page. Per-minute p99 from a few dozen requests is basically the single slowest request. Require a sustained breach, or compute the percentile over a longer window, or both.
  3. Treating drift as an emergency. Drift says the world changed, not that the model is wrong. Route drift alerts to a ticket for someone to investigate. Page only on symptoms users feel, such as errors, latency, or a measured accuracy drop.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1Production should run exactly the image that passed staging. Which practice guarantees that?

  • The same commit can build different images: base-image patches and unpinned packages change between builds.

  • The artifact is immutable, so "what passed staging" and "what runs in production" are the same bytes.

  • Re-testing helps, but it doesn't make the two environments run the same artifact.

Show answer

B. The artifact is immutable, so "what passed staging" and "what runs in production" are the same bytes.

2The new model loads a 2 GB file at startup, which takes 90 seconds. What happens if liveness checks the model is loaded, with a 30-second timeout?

  • Liveness failures trigger restarts. The model never gets 90 seconds, so the container loops. Readiness (or a startup probe) is where "not loaded yet" belongs.

  • That's what a readiness check does. A liveness check restarts instead of waiting.

  • They run from the start unless you configure an initial delay or a startup probe.

Show answer

A. Liveness failures trigger restarts. The model never gets 90 seconds, so the container loops. Readiness (or a startup probe) is where "not loaded yet" belongs.

3Inputs to the late-delivery model show PSI below 0.05 on every feature, but recall measured on delivered orders fell from 0.49 to 0.31. What is the most likely explanation?

  • PSI says the input distributions match training closely, so the inputs haven't moved much.

  • Something changed the relationship, such as road works or a courier shortage. Only outcome-based monitoring can see this.

  • Ten equal-count bins is the standard choice and works fine at these sample sizes.

Show answer

B. Something changed the relationship, such as road works or a courier shortage. Only outcome-based monitoring can see this.

4Why does the canary router hash the customer ID instead of calling random.random() < 0.05?

  • Speed isn't the reason; both are far cheaper than the prediction itself.

  • Random routing would flip a customer between models on every request, which is confusing for users and makes per-customer comparisons meaningless.

  • Over many requests it lands very close to 5%. The problem is consistency per customer, not the overall share.

Show answer

B. Random routing would flip a customer between models on every request, which is confusing for users and makes per-customer comparisons meaningless.

Key takeaways

  • Continuous deployment is safe when every commit builds one immutable, SHA-tagged artifact and the pipeline verifies the new version after deploying.
  • Canary and shadow releases limit who meets a bad model; blue-green makes switching back instant. Route canaries by a stable hash so customers don't flip between versions.
  • Liveness should be trivial. Readiness should prove the expected model version is loaded and still scores a golden input correctly.
  • Monitor latency percentiles, traffic, errors, and saturation, plus input, prediction, and outcome distributions, from one structured log line per prediction.
  • Page on sustained symptoms users feel. Send drift to a ticket, and judge drift by its size (PSI, KS statistic), not its p-value.

#Further reading

  • Monitoring Distributed Systems (opens in a new tab): the SRE book chapter that defines the four golden signals and argues for symptom-based alerting.
  • Configure liveness, readiness, and startup probes (opens in a new tab): the Kubernetes guide, with clear examples of what each probe failure does.
  • Canary release (opens in a new tab): Martin Fowler's short explanation of canaries, including routing by user and the cost of running two versions at once.

m6-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Save a reference profile of the training data next to the model, so monitoring never needs the training set.
  • Log every prediction from FastAPI middleware, including rejected requests and their latency.
  • Compute PSI by hand and the KS test with scipy.stats for each feature, and chart how a shifted distribution looks.
  • Detect concept drift by joining outcomes to predictions, and turn every signal into an OK, ticket, or page decision.

Here is what you'll have at the end: a monitor.py that reads a day of prediction logs and delivered-order outcomes and prints this report.

Every number except latency is the same on any machine; latency depends on yours. To get there, you'll replay a realistic day through the service. Two things happen that afternoon. At 17:00 the company opens a new suburban zone, so many orders travel farther: data drift. At 19:00 a bridge closes, so the same distance suddenly takes longer: concept drift. A good monitor should flag the first for investigation and page someone for the second.

#Step 1: Train, and save a reference profile with the model

Drift is always measured against something. Save that something at training time, in the same folder as the model, so every model version carries its own baseline: ten equal-count bin edges per numeric feature, the share of training rows in each bin, and a 500-value sample for the KS test.

np.unique on the edges matters for whole-number features. items only takes values 1 to 8, so several deciles fall on the same value, and duplicate edges would create empty bins. The first and last edges become ±infinity so live values outside the training range still land in a bin instead of disappearing.

#Step 2: Log every prediction from middleware

The endpoint knows the features and the score; the middleware knows the status code and the total time, including requests that fail validation and never reach the endpoint. So the endpoint leaves its details on request.state, and the middleware writes one line with everything.

This copy loads from models/ to keep the page short. Your Module 4 service loads whatever the champion alias points to through load_alias, and nothing in this lesson depends on which. The log records features and the score, but no customer name, address, or phone number. Keep it that way: logs get copied to many places, and the monitor only needs what the model saw.

#Step 3: Replay a day of traffic

This cell plays the role of a day in production. It builds 900 orders, applies the two afternoon events, sends each order to the API with its order ID as X-Request-ID, and writes the true outcomes that the dispatch system reports once each delivery finishes. A percent or two of requests are malformed, as real traffic always is.

Every request produced exactly one line, including the rejected ones. In production the lines would stream to stdout, and the platform's log collection (Render's log streams, for example) would forward them to storage where this monitor can read them.

#Step 4: The golden signals

pd.read_json(..., lines=True) turns a JSON-lines file into a DataFrame, one row per request. Rejected requests have no features, so their feature columns are NaN.

These latencies are measured in-process, so they're far below what a client across the internet sees; the shape of the distribution is what matters here. The 4xx rate is tracked separately from 5xx on purpose: 422s mean a caller sent bad data, which is worth a ticket to that team, while 5xx means your service failed, which is worth a page.

#Step 5: PSI by hand, against the saved profile

PSI needs the reference fractions (saved in Step 1) and the live fractions in the same bins. A small floor of 0.0001 on each fraction keeps an empty bin from producing log(0).

Split the day by period before computing drift, or the signal gets diluted: half a day of shifted distances averaged with half a day of normal ones looks like a mild change. The hour row is huge in both windows, and that's expected: each window holds only some hours of the day, while the training profile spreads across all of them. That "drift" is just the clock, which is why real monitors compare each window with the same window in the reference, or leave time features out of drift alerts.

#Step 6: The KS test and a picture of the shift

Read the right panel. The KS statistic is the largest vertical gap between the training curve and a window's curve. The afternoon curve sits below the others because a smaller share of its orders are short. PSI and KS agree here, and they usually will on a shift this size; KS uses the exact values, while PSI depends on the bins but is easier to explain in a report.

#Step 7: Join outcomes to catch concept drift

Inputs alone can't reveal concept drift, because the inputs look normal. Outcomes can. Join each delivered order's true result to its prediction by request ID, then compare, per window, the share of orders the model expected to be late (the mean predicted probability) with the share that actually were.

From 17:00 the model expects more lateness, and it's right: the new zone's long trips really are late more often. That's data drift the model handles. After 19:00, actual lateness pulls far ahead of predicted, and recall falls. The model still ranks orders reasonably (AUC holds up better than recall) but its probabilities are now too low, so too few orders cross the 0.5 warning threshold. That's concept drift, and it's the one customers feel.

#Step 8: Rules, decisions, and the finished monitor

Each signal gets a limit and a severity. Symptoms users feel page; signs that the world changed open a ticket. Here is the whole monitor.py, reusing the psi function from Step 5:

The report pages for the bridge closure and opens a ticket for the new zone. Both are right. The new zone needs a human to decide whether to retrain with suburban orders, which can wait until morning. The bridge closure is making the app tell customers "on time" when it isn't, and that can't wait. In production, run this on a schedule (every 15 minutes, say) over a sliding window of recent logs, and send PAGE results to your on-call tool and TICKET results to the issue tracker.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does train.py save reference.json instead of having the monitor load the training CSV?

  • Retraining on new data changes what "normal" means. Storing the profile with the model keeps the baseline matched to the model actually serving, and keeps raw training data out of production systems.

  • You could recompute bins from the CSV every time; it's just slower, and it ties monitoring to wherever the training data lives.

  • ks_2samp accepts samples of any size. 500 is a size that's small to store but large enough to compare.

Show answer

A. Retraining on new data changes what "normal" means. Storing the profile with the model keeps the baseline matched to the model actually serving, and keeps raw training data out of production systems.

2Logging happens in middleware rather than inside predict(). What would be lost if it moved into the endpoint?

  • Requests that fail validation get a 422 before predict() ever runs.

  • Middleware wraps the whole request, so it can time everything and record requests the endpoint never sees.

  • The endpoint has the version too; that's not what would be lost.

Show answer

B. Middleware wraps the whole request, so it can time everything and record requests the endpoint never sees.

3After 19:00, PSI on every feature is similar to the 17:00–18:59 window, but actual lateness is far above predicted. Which response fits?

  • PSI only describes inputs. The inputs didn't change; the outcomes did.

  • Outcome-based signals measure what users experience. Mitigate first (for example, raise predicted risk for affected routes or show a general delay notice), then retrain.

  • Retraining on a few hours of an unusual event, without the CI gates, risks a worse model when the bridge reopens.

Show answer

B. Outcome-based signals measure what users experience. Mitigate first (for example, raise predicted risk for affected routes or show a general delay notice), then retrain.

Key takeaways

  • Store a reference profile (bin edges, fractions, a sample) with every model version, and measure drift against the profile of the model that's actually serving.
  • Log one JSON line per request from middleware, so rejected requests and true latency are captured, and leave personal data out.
  • Compute drift per time window; mixing shifted and normal periods dilutes the signal, and time-of-day features drift every day by design.
  • PSI and KS answer "did the inputs change?"; only joined outcomes answer "is the model still right?"
  • Map every signal to a severity: user-facing symptoms page, changes in the world open tickets.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Compare each hour with the same hour in the reference instead of the whole training day, so the hour feature stops looking like drift every evening.
  • Expose the counters with a Prometheus client library and a /metrics endpoint, and compute p99 from histogram buckets instead of raw logs.
  • Add a per-slice gap (rainy versus dry, short versus long) to measure, so a problem affecting only long orders isn't averaged away.

#Further reading

  • Prometheus: histograms and summaries (opens in a new tab): how production systems compute latency percentiles from bucketed counts, and the trade-offs of each approach.
  • scipy.stats.ks_2samp (opens in a new tab): the reference for the two-sample KS test, including its alternatives and how the p-value is computed.
  • What is data drift in ML? (opens in a new tab): Evidently's guide to drift types and detection methods, with notes on choosing tests for different data sizes.
